course.title: Technical Writing
course.description: How to write documentation that people can use: knowing the reader, choosing the kind of page, writing clear sentences, procedures and reference entries, documenting an API, and testing the result.
course.audience: A capable adult who writes emails and reports well enough and now has to explain a product, process or system to people who did not build it. Engineers, analysts, support staff and career-changers. No documentation tools are assumed; a few lessons read short HTTP, JSON or Markdown snippets.

paragraphs: Most people who write documentation have never been taught to, and it shows in a particular way: the page is accurate and the reader still can't use it. The writer knows the product so well that they can no longer see what a newcomer is missing. This course is about getting that view back, starting with the person who will read the page, what they are trying to do and what they already know.

From there we work through the decisions a documentation writer makes in the order that they come up. We choose the kind of page, set it out so that it can be scanned, and then go down to the words and sentences, where we can measure what we change with a word count or a reading-ease score. Then we turn to the pages that readers follow or look things up on, namely procedures, code samples, reference entries and the description of an HTTP endpoint.

The last lessons are about keeping documentation true: holding it in version control beside the code, reviewing it by running its steps, and testing it with a real reader who is watched, not asked. A few lessons read short snippets of HTTP, JSON and Markdown, and none assumes you have used a documentation tool before.
outcomes: You'll be able to say who a page is for, what they are trying to do, and what they already know.
You'll be able to choose between a tutorial, a how-to guide, a reference page and an explanation, and say why mixing them fails.
You'll be able to turn a passive, vague sentence into a clear one, and measure the change.
You'll be able to write a procedure with one action per step, and a reference entry with every field a reader needs.
You'll be able to document an HTTP API endpoint with its request, response and errors, and test the page with a reader.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on English: Reading, Writing and Rhetoric, How Computers Solve Problems.

concepts.title: Audience
concepts.summary: The people who will read a page, defined by what they want to do and what they already know.

concepts.title: Curse of knowledge
concepts.summary: Once you know something it is hard to imagine not knowing it, so you skip steps a newcomer needs.

concepts.title: Reader goal
concepts.summary: The task the reader is trying to finish, which the page exists to serve.

concepts.title: Tutorial
concepts.summary: A guided lesson that takes a beginner through a project to build skill and confidence.

concepts.title: How-to guide
concepts.summary: Steps for a reader who already knows the basics to reach a specific goal.

concepts.title: Reference
concepts.summary: Accurate, complete, neutral description of a thing's parts, looked up rather than read through.

concepts.title: Explanation
concepts.summary: Discussion of why something is as it is, to deepen understanding.

concepts.title: Front-loading
concepts.summary: Put the main point or action at the start of the page, section or sentence.

concepts.title: Heading outline
concepts.summary: Headings that form a hierarchy a reader can scan and a tool can turn into a contents list.

concepts.title: Lists and tables
concepts.summary: Numbered lists for sequences, bulleted lists for sets, tables for items that share several attributes.

concepts.title: Active voice
concepts.summary: A sentence in which the actor is the subject, so the reader knows who or what does the action.

concepts.title: Consistent terminology
concepts.summary: One name for one thing throughout, because a new word suggests a new thing.

concepts.title: Ambiguous pronoun
concepts.summary: A pronoun such as it or this that could point to more than one earlier item.

concepts.title: One idea per sentence
concepts.summary: A sentence that carries a single idea is easier to read and to test.

concepts.title: Parallel structure
concepts.summary: List items that begin with the same grammatical form read as a set.

concepts.title: Flesch reading ease
concepts.summary: 206.835 − 1.015 × (words per sentence) − 84.6 × (syllables per word); higher is easier.

concepts.title: Editing passes
concepts.summary: Separate passes for content, structure, sentence clarity and then correctness of words and punctuation.

concepts.title: Filler
concepts.summary: Words that carry nothing, such as 'in order to', 'it should be noted that' and 'very'.

concepts.title: Reading aloud
concepts.summary: Voicing a draft exposes tangled sentences and missing steps.

concepts.title: One action per step
concepts.summary: Each numbered step asks for one action, so the reader can do it, check it and place themselves in the list.

concepts.title: Prerequisites
concepts.summary: What the reader needs before step 1: access, tools, versions.

concepts.title: Expected result
concepts.summary: What the reader should see after a step or at the end, so they know it worked.

concepts.title: Minimal sample
concepts.summary: A sample with only what the point needs, small enough to read in one glance.

concepts.title: Runnable sample
concepts.summary: A sample that works when copied, including imports and setup, tested at each release.

concepts.title: Show the output
concepts.summary: Giving the result next to the code lets the reader check their run against it.

concepts.title: Reference template
concepts.summary: Every entry has the same fields in the same order so readers can find a detail without reading.

concepts.title: Parameter description
concepts.summary: Each parameter gets a name, type, whether it is required, default and one-sentence description.

concepts.title: Neutral description
concepts.summary: Reference states what is, without instruction or opinion.

concepts.title: Endpoint
concepts.summary: An HTTP method and path that performs one operation, such as GET /v1/items/{id}.

concepts.title: Status code
concepts.summary: The three-digit number in a response: 2xx success, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.

concepts.title: OpenAPI description
concepts.summary: A machine-readable file describing endpoints, parameters and schemas from which reference pages can be generated.

concepts.title: Docs as code
concepts.summary: Writing documentation in plain text files, reviewed and published with the same tools as code.

concepts.title: Style guide
concepts.summary: Agreed rules for terms, tone and formatting, ideally checked by a linter.

concepts.title: Changelog
concepts.summary: A dated list of changes per release, grouped as added, changed, deprecated, removed, fixed and security.

concepts.title: Documentation usability test
concepts.summary: A reader attempts a real task using only the page while an observer watches without helping.

concepts.title: Task success rate
concepts.summary: Participants who finish the task divided by participants who attempted it.

concepts.title: Feedback loop
concepts.summary: Page ratings, search terms and support tickets that show where docs fail after release.

lessons.title: Who is reading, and why

steps.headline: Once you know something, you can no longer feel how much of it you know, and this is called the curse of knowledge.

lead.text: The engineer's problem has been measured. In 1990 Elizabeth Newton, in her doctoral work at Stanford, asked people to tap out the rhythm of a well-known song on a table while a second person tried to name it from the taps alone. Before the listeners guessed, the tappers were asked how often they expected to be understood, and they said about half the time. In the usual retelling, listeners named 3 songs out of 120.

The tappers weren't being vain. While tapping, each of them could hear the tune in their head, and that made the taps seem to carry it. The listeners heard only knocks. We call this gap the **curse of knowledge**: once you know something, it is very hard to imagine what it is like not to know it.

afterFigure.text: Notice what the curse does to a writer. It doesn't make you write badly sentence by sentence. It makes you leave out the steps and the words that feel too obvious to mention, and those are exactly the ones a newcomer needs.

diagram.alt: Two horizontal bars to the same scale. The expected rate of 50 percent is a long bar and the actual rate of 2.5 percent is a very short one.
diagram.caption: The expected bar is 20 times the length of the actual bar.

steps.headline: A page needs one reader, one goal and a statement of what that reader already knows.

lead.text: If the curse of knowledge is the problem, what is the cure? A writer needs some way to hold the reader's position in mind, and the most practical one is to write it down. Start with the **audience**, the people who will read the page. Then ask what each of them is trying to do, which is the **reader goal**, and what they already know when they arrive, which is their **starting knowledge**. Put the three together in one sentence.

afterFigure.text: Here is a statement for a page about API keys: "A developer who has used a REST API before, wants to send their first authenticated request, and has not yet created a key." Every part earns its place. Because the reader has used a REST API, the page needn't explain what a request is. Because they have no key yet, the page must start with creating one.

steps.headline: Write an audience statement for a page that begins: "Open the console, find the customer, press Reset."

workedSteps.text: The page tells you who it expects to see it. The words "the customer" and "press Reset" point to someone handling customer accounts.
Next find what the page exists to do. Every step leads to one result, a changed password.
Finally find what the page assumes. It never says where the console is or how to open it, so it assumes the reader has used it.
workedSteps.math: starting knowledge: has used the console

workedSteps.text: Join the three parts in one sentence, and check it by asking whether the page could change if one part changed.
workedSteps.math: "A support agent who has used the console before and needs to reset a customer's password."

lead.text: Before we look at skipped steps, try one. The page says: "Navigate to the project folder and run npm start."

reveal.text: The tool that makes npm available is never mentioned, and neither are the terminal or the download of the project. The next screen lists them.

steps.headline: A skipped step is an action the writer performs without noticing, so the way to find one is to list what the reader would have to do.

lead.text: The surest way to catch the curse of knowledge is to do the task the way a newcomer would, writing down every action. Take the line "Navigate to the project folder and run npm start." To the writer it is two actions. To a newcomer it is five: open a terminal, install Node.js, get the project onto the machine, change into its folder, and only then run the command. The figure marks which of them the sentence mentions.

afterFigure.text: Notice that nothing in the sentence is wrong. It is correct, and for the writer it is complete. The problem only appears when you ask who is following it, and that is why the audience statement comes first: it tells you which of these five actions you may leave out. For a reader whose statement says they use a terminal daily, the first one can go.

diagram.caption: Two actions are written; three are left out. The three are the ones a newcomer has to guess.

workedSteps.text: The page says "Deploy by pushing your branch." A newcomer must add the remote, authenticate, create a branch, push it and watch the build.
The page names two of them: creating a branch and pushing it.
Subtract to find how many a newcomer has to guess.

steps.headline: When a page has more than one kind of reader, serve one of them and link to the others.

lead.text: What if the page has to serve both a newcomer and an expert? It is tempting to write for everyone, and the result is a page that suits nobody: the newcomer drowns in details and the expert wades through basics. A better habit is to choose a **primary reader**, write the page for that person, and signpost the rest with links such as "New to keys? Read what a key is first" or "Looking for every option? See the reference."

afterFigure.text: This doesn't mean experts want less. They want less about the basics, but they still need exact details such as the name of an option and its default. So an expert page is shorter in its introduction and just as careful in its facts.

blocks.text: Suppose an engineer has just finished a service and writes the setup page for a colleague who joins the team on Monday. The page says: clone the repository, install the dependencies, and start the server. Those are the steps the engineer takes every morning, and to her they look complete. Now follow the colleague through them. She has to find the repository's address, decide which folder on her laptop will hold it, find out that "install the dependencies" needs a build tool she doesn't have yet, and work out which file starts the server. Three steps on the page have become eight on the screen, and the five that were never written down are the ones she cannot do alone.

What went wrong? The engineer wasn't careless. She wrote down what she knows, and she can no longer feel the gap between what she knows and what the page says. The figure shows the page as written and then the same task as the colleague meets it.

blocks.text: You saw that people who know something badly overestimate what a newcomer can follow, and that the fix is to write the reader down: who they are, what they want and what they already know. The same habit exposes skipped steps, because you can list what a newcomer would actually do and compare it with what the page says.

lessons.title: Four kinds of page

steps.headline: Documentation serves four different needs, and each need is met by a different kind of page.

lead.text: The four readers in the opening are the ones Daniele Procida described in his Diátaxis framework, which sorts documentation by what the reader needs. A **tutorial** teaches a beginner by guiding them through a small project, so that they build skill and confidence. A **how-to guide** gives steps to a reader who already has the basics and wants a particular result. A **reference** describes the parts of a thing accurately and completely, to be looked up rather than read through. An **explanation** discusses why something is as it is, to deepen the reader's understanding.

afterFigure.text: The map arranges the four along two lines. Across the page, the reader is either studying, which means acquiring a skill, or working, which means applying one. Up and down, they are either doing something or knowing something. Each kind sits where one of each meets, and that is why a page can't serve two without compromising both.

lead.text: Test the map on a title. A page is called "Build your first dashboard", and it guides a beginner through one small project.

reveal.text: It sits in the studying and doing corner. The dashboard is only the vehicle for learning the skill.

lead.text: Tutorials and how-to guides are easy to confuse, because both contain steps. Read this opening and decide which it is: "You should already have a working pipeline. To add a retry limit, open the config file and set max_retries."

reveal.text: The first sentence settles it. A page that assumes a working pipeline serves a goal for a reader who already has skill.

steps.headline: Each kind leaves things out on purpose, and that is what keeps it useful.

lead.text: The difference between a tutorial and a how-to guide is easy to miss, so ask what each one is for. A tutorial is a lesson. It chooses one path, shows the reader every step, and says nothing about alternatives, because a beginner who meets three options in step two will stop. A how-to guide is a tool. It assumes the reader knows the basics, names the goal in its title, and gets on with it.

afterFigure.text: Reference leaves out instruction, since a reader checking a default value doesn't want to be taught how to call the function. Explanation leaves out steps, since a reader asking why wants room to think. Seen this way the omissions aren't gaps. They are the reason a reader hunting a parameter can find it in seconds, without a tutorial wrapped around it.

steps.headline: Sort the paragraphs of a mixed "Reset a user's password" page.

workedSteps.text: Read each paragraph and ask what the reader of that paragraph wants. Paragraphs 1 to 5 say "click Users", "choose the account", and so on, so they give steps toward one goal.
Paragraphs 6 to 8 say why passwords expire after 90 days, and what attackers do with old ones, so they answer "why".
Paragraphs 9 to 11 list the fields in the password form with their limits, so they exist to be looked up.

steps.headline: Decide how many paragraphs leave the page once it becomes a how-to guide.

workedSteps.text: The page has 11 paragraphs. Five of them are steps toward one goal, so they stay.
The other six are background and field descriptions, which another kind of page serves better.
Work out how many paragraphs must move.

steps.headline: Mixing the kinds on one page makes every reader wade through the material meant for someone else.

lead.text: Is one long page that serves everyone friendlier? It looks generous, but consider who reads it. The reader mid-task has to scroll past a paragraph on why passwords expire to reach step four. The reader checking a field limit has to find it among the steps. The reader who wants the reasons has them cut into pieces by instructions. Splitting the page doesn't remove any material, so nothing is lost; each reader just reaches theirs without crossing the others'.

afterFigure.text: The how-to keeps its five steps and links to the other two pages at the points where a reader might want them. That link is the useful part. It says to the reader that the reasons exist and where they are, without putting them in the way.

reveal.text: Reference states facts in a regular shape. Anything that teaches, directs or justifies belongs on another page.

lead.text: Change the reader and the kind may change with it. The password page is now for someone who has never used the product and is learning it through this reset.

reveal.text: The same steps can appear on either page. What differs is whether the page assumes skill or builds it.

lessons.nextAction: Make a page easy to scan with headings, front-loading and the right kind of list.

blocks.text: Think about four people who have all opened the documentation for the same product on the same afternoon. One started using it an hour ago and wants to be taught. One is halfway through a task and needs the next step. One is checking whether a setting takes seconds or milliseconds. One keeps wondering why the product works the way it does at all. Could one page serve all four?

It would have to teach, instruct, list facts and discuss ideas at once, and each of those jobs asks for different writing. The teacher wants gentle steps, the person mid-task wants no detours, the one checking a detail wants a table and nothing else, and the curious one wants to be given the time to think. Writers who try to serve all four on one page usually serve none of them well.

intro.whyItMatters: Choosing the kind of page first decides what to include and what to leave out.

recap.keyIdea: Documentation comes in four kinds, tutorial, how-to guide, reference and explanation, and a page does its job when it stays one kind.

blocks.text: You sorted pages by what their reader needs: a tutorial builds skill, a how-to guide finishes a task for someone who has the skill, a reference answers a lookup, and an explanation gives reasons. Each leaves out what would slow its reader down, which is why a page that mixes them makes everyone wade through someone else's material.
When you meet a mixed page, decide what it is for, keep that, and move the rest to the page where it belongs with a link between them.

lessons.title: Structure for finding things

steps.headline: Readers scan before they read, so a page works when its headings and first words can be read on their own.

lead.text: Look at the two versions in the figure. Both contain the same information, but in the first the setting you want is somewhere in a block of twelve lines of text, and in the second a heading, a short introduction and three numbered steps put it where a scanning eye lands. That difference is what we mean by structure, and none of it needs better sentences. It needs the important things to be placed where a reader will look first.

The habit behind this is called **front-loading**: put the main point or the action at the start of the page, the section and the sentence. Journalists call the page-level version the inverted pyramid, in which the conclusion comes first and the detail follows. In a sentence it means writing "Open Settings to change the timeout" and not "To change the timeout, open Settings", so that a reader who stops after three words has still got the instruction.

afterFigure.text: Front-loading is also a kindness to a careful reader. If the point comes first, everything after it is read knowing why it's there.

lead.text: Before we look at how headings are built, decide what a heading on a procedure page, such as "Configure the proxy", has to start with.

reveal.text: The verb gives the reader a task to match against the task in their head. A heading such as "Things to know" gives them nothing to match.

steps.headline: Headings are an outline of the page: verbs for what the reader can do, nouns for the things they can look up.

lead.text: A page's headings, read in order, should work as a contents list, which is how many documentation tools build theirs. That works only when each heading names what is under it and sits at the right level. On a procedure page the headings are tasks, so they begin with verbs: "Create an API key", "Rotate an API key". On a reference page they are the things being described, so they are nouns: "Key length", "Expiry period". Clever headings fail because a scanning reader has no time to decode them.

afterFigure.text: Notice also that a heading answers the question "is this the section I want?" for a reader who hasn't read a word of it. If you could swap it for "Things to know" without losing anything, it wasn't naming the content.

lead.text: A page lists four browsers that the product supports. Nothing about their order matters.

reveal.text: The list type is a small promise to the reader. Numbers promise a sequence, and here there is none to promise.

steps.headline: Choose a structure for three plans that each have a name, a cost and a limit.

workedSteps.text: List what is being described. There are three plans, and each has the same three attributes, so the reader will want to compare them.
Ask whether the order matters. The plans may be compared in any order, so numbers would promise a sequence that isn't there.
Ask whether a reader will compare across the items. They will, and a table lines each attribute up in one column.
Check against the alternative. Bullets would repeat the three attributes in a line of words for each plan, which is hard to compare.

steps.headline: Use a numbered list for a sequence, a bulleted list for a set, and a table for items that share several attributes.

lead.text: Three kinds of structure cover most of what documentation needs. A **numbered list** is for steps that must be done in order, since it lets a reader say which one they have reached. A **bulleted list** is for a set whose order doesn't matter. A **table** is for items that share several attributes, because each attribute gets a column to compare down.

afterFigure.text: The temptation is to turn everything into bullets, and it costs something. A connected explanation, such as why a cache must be cleared first because stale entries would be served, depends on its "because" and its "so". Cut into bullet fragments it keeps the nouns and loses the argument. Keep short paragraphs for reasoning, one topic in each, and use lists only where the content really is a sequence or a set.

steps.headline: Measure how far a sentence hides its action, then move it.

workedSteps.text: The sentence reads "To change the timeout, open Settings." The action is "open".
The words before it are the part a scanner must read first.
Rewrite with the action first: "Open Settings to change the timeout." Now no words come before "open".

reveal.text: The structure follows the content: a sequence gets numbers, a set gets bullets, attributes get a table, and reasoning gets prose.

lessons.orientation: Make a page scannable with front-loading, headings that name content and the right choice of list or table.

blocks.text: A reader arrives at a page on setting up a proxy because something is broken, and what they want is one number: the name of the setting that holds the proxy's address. They won't read the page from the top. Their eyes will run along the first line or two, drop to a heading that looks about right, and then slide down the left edge looking for the setting's name. Eye-tracking studies of web pages, reported by the Nielsen Norman Group in 2006, found this pattern so often that it was named the F-shaped pattern, after the shape the eyes trace.

If that is how the page is going to be read, then the writer's job changes a little. A good page is one whose first words, headings and list items can be read on their own and still get the reader to the answer. A few tools make that happen, and the figure above shows the shape they are written for.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to set out a page so a reader can find an answer by scanning: front-loaded sentences, headings that name the content, and the right list or table.
intro.whyItMatters: Most readers scan first, so a page that can be scanned is a page that gets read.

recap.keyIdea: A page is scannable when it front-loads its points, names its sections with verbs or nouns that say what is under them, and uses numbers, bullets or a table to fit the content.

blocks.text: You saw that readers scan along the top and down the left edge, so the main point belongs at the start of the page, the section and the sentence. Headings then work as an outline, with verbs for tasks and nouns for things to look up, and the choice between numbers, bullets and a table depends on whether the content is a sequence, a set or items with several attributes.
Prose stays where the content is reasoning, because a list cuts the connecting words that make an explanation an explanation.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson goes inside the sentence, to the words that make a page clear or vague.

lessons.title: Clear words

steps.headline: Active voice puts the actor first and the object second, and the reader always learns who does what.

lead.text: Both sentences in the figure say the same thing about the same file. In "The application saves the file", the thing that acts comes first, then its action, then the thing acted on. We call that **active voice**. In "The file is saved by the application" the order is turned round, and we call it **passive voice**. It is longer, and the actor has been pushed to the end where it can be, and often is, dropped, which is how "The configuration file should be edited" arose.

afterFigure.text: A rule of thumb is to ask "by whom?" at the end of a sentence. If the question has an answer that isn't in the sentence, the actor has gone missing, and you should decide whether to put it back.

diagram.caption: Active puts the actor first. Passive puts the object first and the actor last.

reveal.text: Moving it to the front gives "The application saves the file", which is two words shorter.

steps.headline: Passive voice is not wrong, and specific verbs matter as much as the voice they are in.

lead.text: Does this mean every passive sentence is a mistake? It doesn't. "The file is deleted after 30 days" is a good sentence, because the reader needs the rule and not the process that carries it out. Passive earns its place when the actor is unknown or unimportant, or when the object is what the sentence is about. Reach for active when the reader has to act, or has to know who is responsible, which in documentation is most of the time.

The verbs deserve the same attention. "Perform an installation of the package" says what "install the package" says, in more words, because the verb has been turned into a noun and a weak verb added to carry it. In the same way "utilize" can nearly always be "use", and a plain verb tells the reader the same thing faster.

afterFigure.text: So the question to ask isn't whether the sentence is passive. It is whether the reader would be better off knowing who acts, and whether a shorter, plainer verb would carry the same meaning.

lead.text: Words vary in prose for elegance, and we're taught to do it. Try the idea on a technical page: it says "copy the folder", then "open the directory", then "check the location", and all three mean one place.

reveal.text: The next screen shows why. A careful reader takes each new word as a sign of a new thing.

steps.headline: Choose one name for each thing and keep it, because a new word tells the reader there is a new thing.

lead.text: Literary prose varies its words to avoid repetition. Documentation can't, because the reader has no way to know that "folder", "directory" and "location" are one place. The writer's variation reads, to someone who has to act on it, as three places, and the reader will go looking for the other two. The remedy is **consistent terminology**: pick a name for each thing, use it every time, and, if the product's interface uses a particular word, use that one.

afterFigure.text: The same goes for names of things in the product. If the button says Build, the page says Build, not "the compile button" in one place and "the run action" in another.

steps.headline: A pronoun is clear only when exactly one earlier noun could be meant, so replace it with the noun otherwise.

lead.text: Pronouns cause trouble because the writer knows what "it" refers to and the reader has to work it out. In "The script reads the config and writes the log. It fails if missing," the word "it" could mean the script, the config or the log, and "missing" fits only one of them. We call a pronoun like this an **ambiguous pronoun**. The same happens with "this" at the start of a sentence, as in "Click the button. This starts the build." Does "this" mean the click, the button or the fact that you clicked?

afterFigure.text: The cure is almost always to use the noun again. "Click Build. The build starts a new container" has no pronoun, and every sentence in it can be understood on its own.

steps.headline: Count the passive verbs in a short paragraph.

workedSteps.text: The paragraph reads: "The server is restarted. The cache is cleared and the logs are rotated. Then the service starts." Find a form of "to be" with a past participle.
"is restarted" is passive. "starts" is active, because the service does it.
Add up all the passive verbs.

lead.text: Apply the exception. "The file is deleted after 30 days" is passive, and it is good documentation.

reveal.text: Passive is a tool, not a fault. What the reader needs decides whether the actor belongs in the sentence.

lessons.orientation: Turn passive, vague or inconsistent sentences into clear ones with active verbs, one term per thing and no ambiguous pronouns.
lessons.nextAction: Shorten sentences, give each paragraph one topic and measure readability with the Flesch score.

blocks.text: Here is a sentence that could be in almost any set of instructions: "The configuration file should be edited." It reads easily enough, so what is wrong with it? Try to answer a question about it. Who edits the file? You might, or the administrator, or an installer script that runs earlier. The sentence knows, but it doesn't say, and a reader who has to guess will sometimes guess wrong.

Several small habits of this kind account for much of the difference between a page that is clear and one that merely looks correct: leaving the actor out, using three words for one thing, and writing "it" or "this" where it could mean any of several earlier nouns. They are easy to fix once you can see them, and the rest of the lesson is about seeing them.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to rewrite a passive sentence so its actor is clear, use one word for one thing, and replace a vague pronoun with the noun it stands for.
intro.whyItMatters: Clear words cost the writer a little attention and save every reader from guessing.

recap.keyIdea: Name the actor, use one word for one thing, and replace ambiguous pronouns with nouns, keeping passive for sentences where the actor does not matter.

blocks.text: You looked at three habits that make a page look correct and read badly: leaving out the actor, varying a word for style, and using a pronoun that could point to several nouns. Each hides something the reader needs, and each is fixed by saying the thing again, plainly.
Passive voice survives where the actor is unknown or unimportant, because the aim isn't a rule against it but a page that tells the reader who does what whenever that matters.

lessons.title: Sentences, paragraphs and readability

steps.headline: A sentence carries one idea well, and when it carries three, the reader has to hold two of them while waiting for the third.

lead.text: Compare the long sentence in the opening with the same material cut into four, as in the figure: "Does your version predate 2.0, and have you set a proxy in the settings file? That file lives in your home directory. Before you upgrade, back up the file and note down the proxy address. The installer replaces the file and keeps none of the old values." Nothing of substance has been dropped, and each sentence now holds one thing. The first asks the reader to check their situation, the second says where the file is, the third gives the instruction, and the fourth gives the reason. We call that **one idea per sentence**, and it's easy to test: if you can't say what a sentence is about in a few words, it is probably about several things.

afterFigure.text: Notice also that the instruction now sits at the start of its sentence, after only a short condition. Splitting is rarely about making things shorter for their own sake. It is about putting each piece where the reader is ready for it.

reveal.text: Putting the condition first means a reader who isn't updating can skip the line, and doesn't open the menu before finding out.

steps.headline: List items that begin the same way read as a set, and items that change form make the reader stop and re-read.

lead.text: The same idea, that the reader should be able to predict the next piece, applies to lists. In the first list in the figure each item begins with a verb that names an action: install, configure, run. A reader who has understood the first item has understood the pattern of all three. This is **parallel structure**. In the second list, the middle item turns into an -ing form and the last into a passive sentence, so the reader keeps checking whether each item is a step, a heading or a description.

afterFigure.text: Parallel structure also makes errors visible. If three items start with verbs and the fourth starts with a noun, the odd one stands out, and it often turns out to be the one that was left unfinished.

lead.text: A formula for reading difficulty adds two quantities to a fixed starting number: the average number of words in a sentence and the average number of syllables in a word. Before you see it, decide which one a small change will move more.

reveal.text: The next screen gives the formula, and you can see the weights for yourself.

steps.headline: The Flesch reading ease score starts from 206.835 and subtracts a penalty for long sentences and a much bigger one for long words.

lead.text: Rudolf Flesch published his Reading Ease formula in 1948, and it is still the standard quick measure. It takes the average number of words per sentence, W, and the average number of syllables per word, S, and computes 206.835 − 1.015 × W − 84.6 × S. The result is a **Flesch reading ease** score, and a higher score means easier text. Scores in the 60s are usually called plain English, and scores below 30 are very hard.

afterFigure.text: Look at the two cases in the figure. Both have 15 words per sentence, so the sentence term is the same, 15.225. When the words get a tenth of a syllable shorter, the syllable term drops from 126.9 to 118.44, a difference of 8.46, and the score rises from 64.71 to 73.17. A tenth of a syllable is worth more than eight points, while a whole extra word per sentence costs only about one.

Multiply each penalty separately, so that a slip in one doesn't spoil the other.
Subtract both from the starting number.
Round if you are asked to, and read the result against the scale.

lead.text: Use the formula on the opening sentence. As one sentence of 52 words, with 1.6 syllables per word, it scores 206.835 − 52.78 − 135.36, which is about 19. Now cut the same text into four sentences of equal length.

reveal.text: Splitting made no words shorter, and it still lifted the score by roughly 39 points, because sentence length is the only thing that changed.

steps.headline: A readability score measures the length of sentences and words and nothing else, so it can't tell a right instruction from a wrong one.

lead.text: Is a high score a sign of good writing? Look at the two lines in the figure. "Press Save to keep your work" and "Press Save to wipe your work" have the same number of words and the same word lengths, so they score the same, although only one of them matches what the button does. The formula counts letters and sentences. It can't check accuracy, or whether the steps are in order, or whether a word such as "authentication", which is long and also necessary, will be understood by this reader.

afterFigure.text: The score also rewards the wrong thing if you chase it. A string of very short sentences scores well and loses the connections between ideas, which is the "because" and "so" that make a paragraph an explanation. Use the number as a smoke alarm. A low score is a reason to look again at your sentences, and a high score is not proof that they are good.

lessons.nextAction: Edit a draft in separate passes for structure, sentences and words, and measure how much you cut.

blocks.text: Here is a sentence of the kind that turns up in real documentation: If you use a version released before 2.0 and have set a proxy in the settings file, which lives in your home directory, then before you upgrade you should back up that file and note down the proxy address, because the installer replaces the file and keeps none of the old values. It has 52 words and three separate pieces of information, and a reader has to keep the first two in mind while waiting for the instruction, which doesn't arrive until the middle. Read it once, and then try to say aloud what you are meant to do.

Most people find they have to go back to the start. Nothing in the sentence is wrong, and every word does some work, so why is it hard? The reason is that the sentence asks the reader to hold several things at once, and a page is easier to use when it gives them one at a time. Sentences can be split and ordered, lists built in a particular way, and a formula tries to measure how hard text is to read.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to split an overloaded sentence, make a list parallel, and compute a Flesch reading ease score and say what it does and does not tell you.
intro.whyItMatters: Short sentences and a measurable score give you something to check when a page feels hard.

recap.keyIdea: A sentence is clear when it carries one idea, its lists run in parallel, and a Flesch score can check its length without judging whether it is right.

blocks.text: You split a 52-word sentence into four, put conditions before actions, and made list items begin the same way. Then you computed reading ease from words per sentence and syllables per word, and saw that a tenth of a syllable counts for far more than an extra word.
The score is a useful alarm that cannot tell right from wrong, and very short sentences lose the connections that carry an explanation.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson puts these skills into a routine: editing a draft in separate passes, and measuring how much you cut.

lessons.title: Editing a draft

steps.headline: Edit in separate passes, in a fixed order, so that each decision is made before the work that depends on it.

lead.text: Suppose you fix the commas in a paragraph, and then decide the whole paragraph isn't needed. The commas cost you time and taught you nothing. The remedy is to edit in **passes**, each looking for one kind of fault. First, decide what the reader must do or know, and delete the rest. Second, check the order and the headings. Third, work through sentences and words, using the habits from the last three lessons. Fourth, check the small facts: names, numbers, links and any step that refers to another.

afterFigure.text: The order is the point. The first pass can remove paragraphs, so you don't polish them. The second can move them, so you don't tidy words that are about to move. By the fourth pass nothing large will change, and so checking a number can't be undone by a later edit. It also helps to leave the draft alone for a while before the first pass, because you will read it more like a stranger.

reveal.text: Cutting content first means every later pass has less to work on.

lead.text: Editing has to be measured, or it is just a feeling. A paragraph of 40 words is edited down to 28.

reveal.text: That count is the first of two measures. The next screen shows how to turn it into a percentage that can be compared between edits.

steps.headline: Filler is any word the reader would not miss, and the size of a cut is the words removed divided by the words you started with.

lead.text: Look at the 15-word instruction in the figure. The shaded words, "In order", "it is necessary that you" and "the following", can go with no loss, because what the reader has to do is carried by "start the server" and "run". We call words of that kind **filler**. They tend to appear in the same few phrases, such as "in order to", "it should be noted that" and "very", which is why they are worth learning to spot. The 15 words become 7.

afterFigure.text: To measure the cut, take the words removed, 15 minus 7, which is 8, and divide by the length you started with: 8 ÷ 15 is about 0.53. About 53% of the sentence was filler. Dividing by the original length matters, because a cut is a fraction of what you had.

steps.headline: A cut is allowed only if every fact survives, so a warning, a number or a condition stays however short the page gets.

lead.text: Shortness is not the goal. The goal is a page that keeps what the reader needs, and a hurried edit can cut a word that was doing real work. "Do not delete the backup" loses its point if "Do not" goes. "Wait 30 seconds" shortened to "wait" has lost a number the reader acts on, and "version 2.0 or later" is no longer true as "a later version".

afterFigure.text: So each cut gets one test: would the reader do something different without this word? If so, the word is a fact and stays. If not, it is filler and can go, which is why "very" and "in order to" are safe, while "not" never is.

steps.headline: Reading a draft aloud and checking its small facts last catches what a silent read skips.

lead.text: Two habits finish the work. Read the draft aloud, or have someone else read it to you. A sentence that makes you stumble or take a breath in the wrong place is usually tangled, and a step that you have to skip over to make sense of the next one is a step that is missing. The ear picks up what the eye, which has seen the draft many times, has stopped noticing.

afterFigure.text: Then do the fourth pass, which is about small facts. Check that the product name is spelled and capitalised as it appears on screen, that each number matches the software, and that each link still goes where it says. These are the errors a reader finds in seconds and that make them doubt everything else on the page.

lead.text: Put the measure and the rule together. A 50-word paragraph holds 9 words of filler and a 5-word warning. You cut the filler and keep the warning.

reveal.text: Notice that the warning kept the cut from reaching 28%. A careful edit often removes less than the most it could.

lessons.orientation: Edit a draft in four passes, cut filler without losing facts, and measure the cut as a percentage.
lessons.nextAction: Write a numbered procedure with one action per step, the where before the what, and the result stated.

blocks.text: A first draft is a record of what the writer was thinking, and a page is for what the reader needs to do. The two are rarely the same, and the gap shows up as words. Take the sentence "In order to start the server, it is necessary that you run the following command." It has 15 words, and it can be written in seven: "To start the server, run this command." Nothing the reader needs has been lost, and the second version takes less than half the time to read.

The edit was easy to see here because the sentence stood alone. In a whole draft the same padding is spread across pages, and it is much harder to spot, particularly while you are also worrying about commas, headings and whether the steps are in the right order. The way through is to stop doing all of those at once.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to edit a draft in four passes, cut filler without losing a fact, and say how much you cut as a percentage.
intro.whyItMatters: Separate passes stop small fixes from hiding large faults, and a measured cut shows the edit was real.

recap.keyIdea: Edit in four ordered passes, cut only words that carry no fact, and measure the cut as words removed divided by words you started with.

blocks.text: You edited in passes, deciding content first and checking small facts last, so that each decision came before the work that depended on it. Filler such as "in order to" could go, and the size of a cut was the words removed divided by the original length: 8 of 15 words, about 53%.
The cut had one limit. A warning, a number or a condition is a fact, so it stays whatever the length, and reading the draft aloud helps catch a step that has gone missing.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson applies all of this to one kind of page, the procedure, where each step must be a single action the reader can check.

lessons.title: Writing a procedure

steps.headline: Each numbered step should ask for one action, so that the reader can do it, check it and find their place again.

lead.text: The reason is practical. In the figure, the packed step hides which action failed, and the reader has to start again from the top. Split into three steps, a failure at step 3 shows that steps 1 and 2 worked. This is the rule of **one action per step**. It also gives the reader a way back in: someone who looks up from the screen can say "I'm on step 2" and continue from there.

afterFigure.text: Each step also begins with a verb in the imperative, such as "Open", "Select" or "Click", because the reader is being told what to do. A list that starts "Settings should be opened" is longer and makes the reader work out the instruction.

steps.headline: Put the place before the action, because the reader's eyes need to be on the right part of the screen before they act.

lead.text: Compare "In the File menu, click Save" with "Click Save in the File menu". The second tells the reader to find a Save button before they know where it is, and they may click the wrong Save, or spend a few seconds scanning the whole window. The first sends them to the File menu, and the action arrives when they're looking at the right place. The rule is **location first**, and it applies to any step that has both.

steps.headline: A procedure has three parts, in order: what the reader needs, steps that show their result, and help for when something goes wrong.

lead.text: Put the **prerequisites** first, before step 1: the access, the tools and the software versions the reader needs. A reader who learns on step 6 that they need an administrator account has already half-changed their system. Then state the **expected result** for any step where the reader can't tell by looking whether it worked, as in "The status changes to Running within 30 seconds." Without that line, a silent failure and a slow success look the same.

afterFigure.text: Troubleshooting comes after the steps, not inside them. A reader in the middle of a task wants the next step, and the reader whose step has failed knows to look below the list.

blocks.text: Take a step from a procedure that looks perfectly tidy: "Open Settings, select Network, and click Reset." It's short, it keeps the list compact, and every word in it is needed. Now suppose the reader follows it and nothing happens. Did Settings fail to open, was there no Network entry on their version, or did the Reset button do nothing? The step contains three possible failures, and the reader can't tell which one they met.

A procedure is the one kind of page that a reader follows while doing something else, with their eyes going back and forth between the page and the screen. That changes what good writing means. The page has to let the reader do one thing, check it, and find their place again, and it has to tell them what they will see when each thing works.

recap.keyIdea: A procedure lists prerequisites first, asks for one action per step with the place before the action, and states what the reader should see.

blocks.text: You took a packed step apart and saw that a failure at the end of one tells the reader nothing, whereas three single-action steps show where they got to. Each step starts with a verb, puts its location or condition first, and, where the reader cannot tell by looking, ends with the result they should see.
Prerequisites go before step 1 so that no one discovers a missing tool halfway through, and troubleshooting goes after the list so that it stays out of the way until it is needed.

lessons.title: Examples and code samples

steps.headline: A good sample holds only what its point needs, so the reader can read it in one glance.

lead.text: Samples grow because the real code they came from was large. A page might show 40 lines to teach one idea, and the reader has to work out which 8 matter. A **minimal sample** is trimmed to those 8: the one call being taught, the setup it can't work without, and nothing else. The test for each line is whether the reader would miss it. A line for logging, or for a feature the page isn't about, is a line the reader has to read, wonder about and rule out.

lead.text: Measure one trim. A sample has 40 lines and the point needs only 8 of them.

reveal.text: Trimming also changes the reader's job from finding the point to checking it.

lead.text: Before we make a sample complete, consider the failure the opening described: a sample that calls json.loads with no import line.

reveal.text: The reader's real problem isn't the error name, which is easy to read. It is that they think the mistake is theirs.

steps.headline: A sample should run exactly as it is copied, with every import in place and every value either real or clearly marked as a stand-in.

lead.text: The fix for the opening's error is one line, `import json`, and the lesson is a general one. A **runnable sample** is complete: it includes its imports and setup, and it works when the reader copies it. This only stays true if someone tests it, ideally automatically at each release, because software changes and an untested sample slowly stops working.

afterFigure.text: Secrets and settings need care. Never put a real key in a sample, and don't write "foo" or "xxx" either, since they don't say what belongs there. Use a **stand-in** that names what to supply, such as YOUR_API_KEY, and say once, near the sample, that it must be replaced.

lead.text: Pick the best header line for a sample that calls an API with a key.

reveal.text: The best stand-in is both obviously fake and self-explanatory.

steps.headline: Put the output next to the sample, so the reader can tell whether their run did what the page says it should.

lead.text: A sample that stops at the command leaves the reader guessing: did it work, and what should they have seen? Show the result immediately after the code, as the second view of the figure does with the JSON the call returns. The reader can then compare line by line, and a difference between what they got and what the page shows is the start of a diagnosis.

afterFigure.text: Explain the idea once, in a sentence before or after the sample, instead of commenting on every line. A sample where each line carries a comment is harder to read than the code, and the comments tend to repeat what the code already says.

steps.headline: Make this sample complete: data = json.loads('{"a": 1}') then print(data['a']).

workedSteps.text: Run it in your head in an empty file. The first line uses json, which hasn't been defined, so Python raises NameError.
Add the missing import above the first line.
Check that every value is real or marked as a stand-in. Here the string is a real value, so nothing needs replacing.
Add the output the reader should see, and the sample is complete.

steps.headline: Work out the output of a complete sample.

workedSteps.text: The sample is: import json, then data = json.loads('{"a": 1, "b": 2}'), then print(data['b']). The import makes json available.
json.loads turns the text into a dictionary with the keys a and b.
Print looks up the key b. Work out the number printed.

lead.text: Apply the same judgement to a new sample. It teaches how to set a timeout on a client.

reveal.text: A line that the point doesn't need is a cost to every reader, however harmless it is in the original program.

lessons.orientation: Write a minimal, runnable sample with stand-ins and its output shown.
lessons.nextAction: Write a reference entry to a fixed template with name, purpose, parameters, returns, errors and an example.

blocks.text: Here is a code sample that someone might copy from a page of documentation: two lines, one that loads some JSON with json.loads and one that prints a value from it. It looks complete and it was probably tested, by a writer who already had the json module imported in their editor session. A reader who pastes it into an empty file gets an error on the first line: the name json is not defined.

The reader's first thought isn't that the page is wrong. It is that they have done something wrong, and they may spend twenty minutes checking their installation. A code sample is a promise that the reader can copy it and see what the page says they will see, and the way to keep that promise is with the least code that will do it.

intro.whyItMatters: A sample is a promise that the reader can copy it and see what the page says, so it has to run.

recap.keyIdea: A code sample holds only what its point needs, runs exactly as copied, uses labelled stand-ins and shows its output.

blocks.text: You saw that a sample with a missing import fails in front of the reader, who then blames themselves. The cure is a sample trimmed to the lines that matter, complete enough to run as copied, with stand-ins such as YOUR_API_KEY in place of secrets, and its output shown beside it.
Testing it at each release keeps the promise true, and one sentence of explanation does more than a comment on every line.

lessons.title: Reference pages

steps.headline: Every reference entry has the same fields in the same order, so that a reader who finds one fact knows where the others are.

lead.text: Does the template matter if the writer is careful? It does, because the reader isn't reading the entry; they are looking for a fact in it. A reader who has used one entry has learned the layout of every other, if the layout is fixed. The **reference template** for a function has six fields: its name, its purpose in one sentence, its parameters, what it returns, the errors it can raise, and an example. The order never changes.

afterFigure.text: The template also makes gaps visible. If one entry has no errors field, the reader can't tell whether the function never fails or the writer forgot. Checking each entry against six fields is a fast review that a script can do.

reveal.text: A field that is absent isn't neutral. It looks like an answer, and the reader has to decide what it means.

lead.text: Now look inside the parameters field. A reader asks what happens if they leave the retries option out.

reveal.text: The next screen builds the parameter table around the facts readers look up, and this one is near the top of the list.

steps.headline: A parameter row has five columns, and the description states what the parameter is, with its unit, in a neutral voice.

lead.text: Each parameter gets one row: its name, its type, whether it is required, its default and a one-sentence description. In the figure the retries row reads "retries, integer, no, 3, tried again after a failure", so a reader who wants to know what happens when it is omitted reads along one row and has it. A table rather than prose lets them scan down a column too, to see which parameters are required.

afterFigure.text: Reference is neutral: it says what is true and doesn't instruct or advise. "The number of seconds to wait for a response before the request fails" is a description. "You should set this high on slow networks" is advice, and belongs in a how-to. Notice that the description gives the unit, seconds, because a bare 30 can mean seconds or milliseconds.

blocks.text: A reader has a call that sometimes fails and they want to know one thing: what happens if they leave the retries option out? They didn't come to learn what retrying is, and they haven't any use for the history of the library. They want to find the word "retries" and read the default beside it. If the page puts that fact in the middle of a paragraph, they have to read the paragraph, and if it omits the default because it seemed obvious, they have to run the code and see.

This is what a reference page is for, which the second lesson called a page that is looked up and not read through. What makes lookup quick is regularity: every entry has the same fields in the same order, so that once you've found one you know where the rest are. That is the whole idea of a reference template, and the lesson shows what goes in one.

blocks.text: You saw that lookup depends on regularity: the same six fields in the same order, and a parameter row with five columns that put the default beside the name. A description states what is true, with its unit, and doesn't advise; advice goes in a how-to and reasons in an explanation, both reached by a link.
The template also shows what is missing, since an empty field can be counted and a gap in prose can't.

steps.headline: An endpoint page gives the method and path, who may call it, what goes in, what comes out and what can go wrong, in that order.

lead.text: An **endpoint** is an HTTP method and a path that together perform one operation, such as GET /v1/items/{id}. The method says what kind of operation it is, and the path says on what. A reader who comes to the page for one endpoint wants six things: what it does, the method and path, how to authenticate, the parameters, what the response looks like, and an example. The figure shows them in the order a reference template uses.

steps.headline: A status code is the three-digit number that starts every response, and its first digit tells you whether the request worked.

lead.text: Every HTTP response begins with a **status code**, defined in RFC 9110 and a few later documents. The first digit sorts them into families. Codes starting with 2 mean success, those starting with 4 mean the client sent something wrong, and those starting with 5 mean the server failed. An API page needs a short list from them: 200, 201 and 204 for success; 400, 401, 403, 404 and 429 for the client's errors; and 500 for the server's.

afterFigure.text: Choosing the code that matches is part of the documentation. A 200 for a created item is accurate but less exact than 201, and a 400 for an expired key points the reader at their request when the fault is their credentials. Use the buttons to see each family.

steps.headline: Document each error with its code, its cause and what the reader should do, and keep 401 and 403 apart.

lead.text: The error rows are the heart of the Responses section. Each gets its status code, a one-line cause and the fix. The commonest confusion is between 401 and 403. A 401 means the request lacks valid credentials: the key is missing, wrong or expired, and the server can't tell who is asking. A 403 means the credentials are valid but don't allow this action, so the server knows who is asking and still refuses.

afterFigure.text: The fixes differ, which is why the page can't treat them alike. For a 401 the reader gets a new or refreshed key. For a 403 a new key would not help, since they need the permission added. Put a single error format on every response, with a code, a message and a hint for the fix, and document it once.

steps.headline: An OpenAPI file describes endpoints in a machine-readable way, and reference pages can be generated from it, but the prose around it is still needed.

lead.text: Many teams keep their endpoint facts in an **OpenAPI description**: a file listing each path, its methods, its parameters and its responses. In the snippet, the lines under responses declare the four codes that POST /v1/items can return. Tools turn a file like this into reference pages, which keeps the facts consistent with the product.

afterFigure.text: What a generated page can't supply is the guidance. The file says that 401 is "key is expired", and a person has to write what the reader does next, when to use the endpoint and how it fits with others. So the file gives the table, and the writer provides the sentences around it.

blocks.text: Suppose an API page documents what a call returns when everything works: you send a POST to /v1/items with a name, and you get back the new item. It is accurate and it is tidy, and nearly all of it is the part a reader will get right on their first try. Then the reader's key expires, the call returns a 401, and the page says nothing about what a 401 means or what to do. They have the answer to a question they didn't have and none for the one they do.

Documenting one endpoint well makes the failures as findable as the successes. The two figures that matter most are the status line, the three-digit number at the top of every response, and the error body that follows it. Everything else on the page is a set of facts a reader can look up, in the template of the previous lesson.

intro.whyItMatters: Readers look up errors at the moment something goes wrong, so the failure cases must be as easy to find as the success.

recap.keyIdea: An endpoint page covers purpose, method and path, authentication, parameters, responses and an example, with each error given its status code, cause and fix.

blocks.text: You documented an endpoint by its method and path and then listed what it can return: 201 for creation, 204 for a delete with nothing to say, and the errors a client causes, 400, 401, 403, 404 and 429. The difference between 401 and 403 carries the lesson, because one needs a new key and the other needs a new permission.
An OpenAPI file can generate the table, and the writer supplies what the reader does about each row.

lessons.title: Docs as code and review

steps.headline: Docs as code means writing documentation in plain text, kept in version control and shipped through the same reviewed process as the product.

lead.text: The pages are plain-text files, usually Markdown, in the repository beside the code. A change to either goes through a **pull request**, in which a teammate reads it before it is merged. Because the files are text, the same tools work on them: you can see exactly what changed between versions, go back to an earlier one, and run automatic checks whenever someone proposes an edit. This arrangement is what people call **docs as code**.

afterFigure.text: The gain is that a change to the flag and the change to its page can travel in one pull request, so the reviewer sees both at once and neither can be forgotten. Step through the path in the figure: the docs follow the same road as the code, and every stop on it is a chance to catch a fault.

reveal.text: Review is the step the wiki in the opening was missing.

steps.headline: A style guide records the team's rules for terms, tone and formatting, and a linter checks them on every change.

lead.text: Teams that write together need agreed rules, such as whether to say "select" or "click on", whether to use "please" in instructions, and how headings nest. These form a **style guide**. A written guide helps, but reviewers can't remember all of it, and checking it by eye is tedious work. So the rules that can be checked by machine are given to a **linter**, a tool that reads the files and reports each break with its file and line number, as the figure shows. Prose linters such as Vale do this for documentation.

afterFigure.text: Automation frees the human reviewer. Once the linter has dealt with terms and formatting, the person reading the pull request can spend their attention on what a machine can't judge: whether the page suits its reader and whether the steps work.

lead.text: Consider what a review can see. A how-to has 12 commands. A proofreader finds no errors. Someone else then runs all 12, and 11 of them succeed.

reveal.text: The next screen builds a checklist around what that second reviewer did.

steps.headline: A docs review tests whether the page works, and proofreading is only a small part of it.

lead.text: Treating review as proofreading misses the point. A reviewer who runs the steps finds the missing flag, the renamed option and the command that only works on the author's machine, and a proofreader can't see any of them because the page reads well. A useful checklist has four questions: does the page match its audience statement, is each fact correct for this version, do the steps run as written, and do the links go where they say.

afterFigure.text: Documentation also has to stay matched to the product. If a page describes version 2.0, keep it with the 2.0 code, and when 3.0 ships, branch the docs with it, so that a reader on the older version isn't told about options that don't exist for them.

steps.headline: A changelog lists the changes in each release under six headings, written for the people who use the product.

lead.text: A **changelog** isn't a copy of the commit log. The commit log is written for the developers, with messages such as "wip" and "refactor: rename helper", most of which no user could act on. A changelog gives a dated heading for each release, and below it the changes grouped under Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed and Security, which is the scheme the Keep a Changelog project recommends. Each entry says what changed for the user and, where they must do something, what that is.

afterFigure.text: The grouping is the useful part. A reader upgrading looks first under Removed and Security, because those are the headings that can break their setup or need quick action, and a long list in time order would hide them.

blocks.text: A command-line tool renames a flag from --out to --output, and the change goes through the usual process: a developer writes it, a colleague reviews it, the tests pass, and it ships. The setup guide still says --out. It lives in a wiki that nobody reviewed, and no test knows it exists, so the first sign of the mistake is a reader's support ticket two weeks later.

The cause is where the page lives. Code is written in plain text, kept in version control, changed through reviewed proposals and checked automatically before it ships, and documentation that sits outside all of that falls behind it. The remedy is to give the documentation the same home, which is what people mean by treating docs as code.

diagram.alt: Two arrangements for documentation. In the first the docs live in a separate wiki with no review, away from the code. In the second a docs folder sits inside the product repository, so a change to the code and its page go through one pull request.

intro.whyItMatters: Documentation that travels with the code is reviewed with it, and so stays true to it.

recap.keyIdea: Docs as code keeps pages in version control, checks style with a linter, reviews by running the steps, and records changes for users in a changelog.

blocks.text: You followed a docs change along the path a code change takes: a pull request, automatic checks from a linter that enforces the style guide, and a review that runs the steps, since proofreading can't tell that a command fails. Together they keep a page in step with the product it describes.
The changelog tells users what changed under six headings, and the entries are written for them, which is why it isn't a copy of the commit log.

lessons.title: Testing documentation with readers

steps.headline: A documentation test puts a real reader in front of the page with a real task, and an observer who watches and does not help.

lead.text: The test has three parts: a task, a participant and an observer. First choose one page and one task that it should enable, such as installing the tool or rotating a key. Then recruit someone who matches the audience statement you wrote in the first lesson, because a colleague who built the product will skip the very steps you want to test. Then have them try the task using only the page, while an observer writes down where they stop, hesitate or go back, and says nothing.

afterFigure.text: That silence is the hard part. When the reader frowns, you will want to explain, and once you do, the test is over, because the real reader never gets an explanation. Everything you learn from this **documentation usability test** comes from the moment the reader is stuck.

lead.text: Count the result of a test. Six of eight participants finish the task.

reveal.text: The next screen sets out the rule for the percentage and for locating where the others stopped.

steps.headline: The task success rate says how many readers finish, and the first point of failure says where the others stopped.

lead.text: Two numbers come out of a test. The **task success rate** is the number who finished divided by the number who attempted the task, expressed as a percentage. If 8 of 10 finish, the rate is 80%. The second number is a place: the step where the others stopped, which is the **first point of failure**. In the figure, ten readers start, all ten reach step 3, and two stop at step 4, so the drop shows at once.

afterFigure.text: Both numbers are small, and both are useful because they are concrete. The two readers stopped at step 4 because the page assumed a tool was already installed, which is the curse of knowledge from the first lesson showing up in a measurement. A rate by itself tells you something is wrong. The point of failure tells you what.

steps.headline: Fix the failure that stops the most readers first, and let the count decide, not the order of the page.

lead.text: A test often finds several faults. In the figure, six readers stopped at step 4 and one stopped at step 7. It is tempting to fix whichever is easiest, or whatever you noticed first, but the count gives a better order. Fixing step 4 helps six readers and fixing step 7 helps one, so step 4 comes first, and when it is fixed you test again to see where the next drop falls.

afterFigure.text: The order of the tests also matters. Retesting with new participants is better than asking the same people to try again, since they now know what the page meant. A handful of readers is usually enough to find the main faults, and the repeated tests show whether each fix worked.

steps.headline: After release, ratings, search terms and support tickets keep telling you where the docs fail.

lead.text: A test is one sample of readers. Once the page is public, other signals take over. Page ratings say which pages disappoint. Search terms show what readers look for and don't find. Support tickets show the questions the docs did not answer, and a cluster of tickets on one error is a hint that the troubleshooting page lacks it. Together these form a **feedback loop**: you publish, readers use the page, the signals come back, and you fix the page.

afterFigure.text: Read the signals with care. A page with few views might be unneeded, but it might just be hard to find, and the search terms and tickets show which. Thirty tickets a month on one error, falling to six after the error is documented, is a result you can measure and report.

diagram.alt: A loop of four boxes: publish the page, readers use it, signals such as ratings, searches and tickets, then fix the page, which leads back to publish.
diagram.caption: After release, the loop continues. Ratings, search terms and support tickets show where the docs fail.
