lead.text: Measure a fix with the signal that comes back. Thirty tickets a month on one error fall to six after the error is added to the troubleshooting page.

reveal.text: A fall of this size shows the fix worked, and it gives you a figure to report.

lead.text: Apply the caution about signals. A page gets few views, yet readers keep asking questions that it answers.

reveal.text: A signal needs a second look before you act on it. Few views might mean the page is not needed, or that readers can't find it.

lessons.orientation: Plan a documentation test with a reader, compute a task success rate and decide what to fix first.
lessons.nextAction: Write a page for a named reader, choose its kind, structure it, edit it, document an endpoint and test it with a real reader.

blocks.text: Ask someone who has just used a page whether it was clear, and most will say yes. They want to be polite, and the page did get them somewhere, or they think it did. What they cannot tell you is what they didn't understand, since a reader doesn't notice a gap that they've filled with a guess. So a question about clarity yields a lot of reassurance and very little information.

Watching someone try to finish a task produces something different, because you see what they do and not what they say. When a reader reaches step 4 and stops, you know exactly where the page failed, and you can see whether the cause is a missing prerequisite, a term they didn't know or a step that assumed a skill. That kind of test can be run, its results counted, and what to fix first decided.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to plan a test with a real reader, compute the task success rate, find the first point of failure and choose which fix comes first.
intro.whyItMatters: A test with a real reader tells you what a page does, which no amount of rereading can.

recap.keyIdea: Watch a real reader attempt a task, compute the success rate and the first point of failure, and fix the failure that stops the most readers first.

blocks.text: You tested a page by watching a reader who matched the audience statement try a task without help, and you counted the result as a success rate, with the step where the others stopped. The count decided the order of fixes, so the failure that stopped six readers came before the one that stopped one.
After release the loop continues through ratings, search terms and support tickets, which you read with care, since a page with few views may be hard to find and not unneeded.

questions.prompt: The tappers expected listeners to name the song 50% of the time, and in the retelling 3 of 120 listeners did. About how many times higher was the expectation than the result?
hints: Start by turning 3 of 120 into a percentage.
Divide 3 by 120 and multiply by 100.
Now divide the expected 50% by that result.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 of 120 is 2.5%, and 50 ÷ 2.5 = 20, so the expectation was twenty times too high.

questions.onCorrect: The expectation was 20 times the result. Newton's own dissertation counts 2 of 150 listeners, so the gap there is even larger.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the result by the expectation. Put the larger figure, 50, on top.
That is the difference between the two percentages. The question asks how many times higher, which needs a division.

questions.prompt: The line "run npm start" assumes the reader has already installed a program. Which one, if npm is the tool that runs on top of it?
hints: npm is the package manager that ships with a particular JavaScript runtime.
The runtime's name begins with the word for a point in a network.
questions.onCorrect: The instruction is short because the writer's machine already has Node.js. A newcomer's may not, and the page never says so.

misconceptions.feedback: Neither of those provides npm. The tool is the JavaScript runtime that npm ships with.

questions.prompt: The statement "A support agent who wants to reset a customer's password" names a reader and a goal. Which third part does it leave out?
hints: A statement has three parts: who, what they want, and one more.
The part you most need in order to decide which steps to include.
questions.onCorrect: Without starting knowledge the writer cannot tell which steps are obvious to this reader and which must be written out.

misconceptions.feedback: The reader is already named, as a support agent. The missing part is about what that person already knows.
The goal is there: reset a customer's password. Look for the part about prior experience.

questions.prompt: The task the reader is trying to finish, and which the page exists to serve, is called the reader's what?
hints: It is what the reader wants to have done when they leave the page.
questions.onCorrect: A page earns its place by getting the reader to their goal, which is why the goal belongs in the audience statement.

questions.prompt: A page says "Deploy by pushing your branch." A newcomer actually has to do five things: add the remote, authenticate, create a branch, push it and watch the build. The page names two of them. How many go unwritten?
hints: Count what the newcomer must do, then what the page says.
The total is five and the page names two.
Subtract the written actions from the total.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 − 2 = 3 actions are left for the reader to guess.

questions.onCorrect: Each unwritten action is a place where a newcomer stops, and the writer rarely notices because the writer does them without thinking.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number the page does name. The question asks for the ones it leaves out.

questions.prompt: The same page is now for a senior administrator who has rotated keys for years and wants only the exact option names. Which edit to the audience statement fits?

choices.label: Change the goal to "learn what a key is"
Change the starting knowledge to "has rotated keys before" and keep the goal
Drop the statement, since experts need no audience
Describe the reader as "everyone who uses keys"

hints: Which of the three parts differs for this reader?
The task is the same, so something else moves.

acceptedIdeas: Change the starting knowledge to "has rotated keys before" and keep the goal
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Change the starting knowledge to "has rotated keys before" and keep the goal

questions.onCorrect: Experts want less about the basics but still need exact details, so only the starting knowledge changes.

misconceptions.feedback: The goal is still to rotate a key. It is the starting knowledge that has changed.
Experts are an audience too. They need fewer basics but exact details.
A mixed reader leads to a page that suits nobody. Keep one primary reader.

questions.prompt: In Newton's tapping study as retold, 3 of 120 listeners named the song. What percentage is that?
hints: Divide 3 by 120.
That gives a decimal; a percentage is that decimal times 100.
0.025 times 100 is the answer.
questions.onCorrect: Tappers had predicted 50%, so what the listener experienced was a fraction of what the tapper imagined.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fraction. Multiply by 100 for a percentage.
Check the decimal place: 3 ÷ 120 is 0.025.

questions.prompt: Which is the best audience statement for a page on resetting passwords?

choices.label: A support agent who has never used the admin console and needs to reset a customer's password

hints: A good statement names who, what they want and what they know.
Pick the one with all three.

acceptedIdeas: A support agent who has never used the admin console and needs to reset a customer's password
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A support agent who has never used the admin console and needs to reset a customer's password

questions.onCorrect: It names a reader, a goal and a starting point, so every later choice about the page can be checked against it.

misconceptions.feedback: "Everyone" gives the writer nothing to decide with, so the page ends up serving nobody.
This names a kind of person but neither a goal nor what they know.
A group name is not a statement: it lacks the goal and the starting knowledge.

questions.prompt: The difficulty of imagining not knowing what you know is called the curse of what?
hints: The word is the thing the writer has too much of.
questions.onCorrect: Because the curse is invisible from the inside, the fix is to check the page against a real reader.

questions.prompt: A page is titled "Build your first dashboard". It guides a beginner through one small project from start to finish. Which of the four kinds is it?
hints: It teaches a newcomer by having them do something together with the page.
Its aim is to build skill and confidence, and not just to finish a job.
questions.onCorrect: A tutorial is judged by what the learner can do afterwards. The dashboard is only the vehicle.

misconceptions.feedback: A how-to guide assumes the reader already has the skill and wants a result. A guided first project for a beginner teaches the skill instead.

questions.prompt: A page begins: "You should already have a working pipeline. To add a retry limit, open the config file and set max_retries." Which of the four kinds is it?
hints: Does the reader get taught from scratch, or does the page assume skill?
It serves a specific goal for someone who can already do the basics.
questions.onCorrect: A how-to guide starts from a reader who has the skill and wants one result, and it skips everything that would slow them down.

misconceptions.feedback: A tutorial would walk a beginner through a project. This page assumes a working pipeline and serves one goal.

questions.prompt: A reader is hunting for the allowed values of one parameter. Which kind of page serves that reader best?
hints: The reader is looking something up, not reading through.
questions.onCorrect: Reference is built for lookup: complete, accurate and neutral, with no teaching around the facts.

misconceptions.feedback: Neither is built for lookup. The reader would have to read through a story or a discussion to find one value.

questions.prompt: A mixed page has 11 paragraphs: 5 are steps for resetting a password, 3 are background on why passwords expire, and 3 describe fields. If the page becomes a how-to guide, how many paragraphs must move to other pages?
hints: Decide which paragraphs belong on a how-to guide.
Only the steps do, and there are 5 of them.
Subtract 5 from 11.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 5 steps stay. 11 − 5 = 6 paragraphs move: 3 of background and 3 of fields.

questions.onCorrect: Background goes to an explanation and fields go to reference, with links left behind in the how-to.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number that stay. The question asks how many leave.
That is only one of the two groups that move. Add the other.

questions.prompt: Which sentence belongs on a reference page for a function?

choices.label: "timeout (integer, default 30): seconds to wait before the call fails."
"Let's build a small program that calls the function."
"We chose a default because slow networks were common."
"First, open your editor and create a new file."

hints: Reference is neutral and complete, like a dictionary entry.
Look for the sentence that only states a fact.

acceptedIdeas: "timeout (integer, default 30): seconds to wait before the call fails."
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: "timeout (integer, default 30): seconds to wait before the call fails."

questions.onCorrect: Reference states facts in a regular shape so a reader can find one quickly, and leaves instruction and reasons to other pages.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how a tutorial opens. Reference does not teach by building something.
That is explanation: it says why. Reference states what is true and nothing more.
That is an instruction for a how-to or a tutorial. Reference describes, it does not direct.

questions.prompt: The password page is rewritten for someone who has never used the product and is learning it by resetting a first password under the page's guidance. Which kind is that page now?
hints: The reader changed from skilled to beginner.
The page now teaches a skill as well as finishing a task.
questions.onCorrect: The task is the same, but the aim has moved from getting the result to building the skill, and that changes the kind.

misconceptions.feedback: A how-to guide assumes skill. For a reader learning from scratch the same material has to teach that skill.

questions.prompt: A page lists every parameter of a function with its type and its default value. Which of the four kinds is it?
hints: Readers look things up on this page rather than read through it.
questions.onCorrect: Because readers consult it, a reference page keeps the same shape for every entry.

misconceptions.feedback: A how-to guide takes the reader through steps to a goal. A list of parameters is looked up.

questions.prompt: A page called "Why we use eventual consistency" discusses the reasons behind a design. Which of the four kinds is it?
hints: Its aim is to deepen understanding.
questions.onCorrect: Explanation takes time over reasons and trade-offs, which would interrupt a reader who is mid-task.

misconceptions.feedback: Reference states what is true. This page discusses reasons and trade-offs.

questions.prompt: A how-to page keeps pausing for two paragraphs of background. What is the best fix?

choices.label: Move the background to an explanation page and link to it

hints: Ask what the reader mid-task needs.
The background is valuable, but it belongs to a different reader.

acceptedIdeas: Move the background to an explanation page and link to it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Move the background to an explanation page and link to it

questions.onCorrect: The how-to stays short, and the reader who wants the background has somewhere to go from a link.

misconceptions.feedback: The steps are the reason the page exists. The background is what is out of place.
More material makes it harder for a reader mid-task to find the next step.
Reference is for lookup. Converting the page would drop the steps without solving the mix.

questions.prompt: A heading on a procedure page should start with a particular kind of word, as in "Configure the proxy". Which kind?
hints: Procedure headings name what the reader will do.
In "Configure the proxy", which word is the action?
questions.onCorrect: A verb-led heading tells a scanning reader what the section lets them do. Nouns suit reference pages, where the reader looks up a thing.

misconceptions.feedback: Nouns suit reference headings, where the reader looks up a thing. A procedure heading names an action.

questions.prompt: A page lists four browsers that the product supports. The order does not matter. Which list type fits?
hints: Does any item need to come before another?
A numbered list would imply a sequence.
questions.onCorrect: Bullets show a set whose order carries no meaning, while numbers promise a sequence the reader may then try to follow.

misconceptions.feedback: Numbers promise a sequence. These four browsers can be read in any order, so a plain bullet list is the honest choice.

questions.prompt: Three plans each have a name, a price and a user limit. Which structure shows them best?
hints: Each item has several attributes that readers will compare.
questions.onCorrect: A table puts each attribute in its own column, so a reader can compare prices down one column without rereading sentences.

misconceptions.feedback: Bullets would repeat the three attributes for every plan in a row of words. Something that lines them up in columns lets them be compared.

questions.prompt: In the sentence "To change the timeout, open Settings." how many words come before the word "open"?
hints: Count from the first word.
Stop at "open" and do not count it.
The four words are To, change, the, timeout.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: "To", "change", "the" and "timeout," make four words before "open".

questions.onCorrect: Rewritten as "Open Settings to change the timeout", the action comes first and no words precede it.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts "open" itself. The question asks for the words before it.
Check whether you counted "To" at the start.

questions.prompt: Two sentences explain why the cache must be cleared first: stale entries would be served, so the new settings would seem to have no effect. Which treatment keeps that reasoning?

choices.label: A table of causes and effects

hints: Which treatment keeps connecting words such as "so"?
A list breaks a sentence into separate items.
questions.onCorrect: Connected reasoning needs connecting words, so prose suits it, and lists suit sequences and sets.

misconceptions.feedback: Fragments drop the "because" and the "so" that carry the reasoning.
A table suits items with shared attributes. This is a single chain of reasons.
Numbers promise steps, and this explains a reason.

questions.prompt: Steps that must be done in order should be set as what kind of list?
hints: The order matters, and the reader may need to say which step they reached.
questions.onCorrect: Numbers let a reader say "I'm at step four" and let a tool keep the place when the list is interrupted.

misconceptions.feedback: Bullets suggest a set with no order. Steps that must run in order need numbers.

questions.prompt: Which is the clearest heading for a page that tells a reader how to replace an API key?
hints: The heading should name the task and start with a verb.
Choose the one that tells you what you could do after reading the section.
questions.onCorrect: A heading that names the action lets a reader decide in a glance whether this is the section they came for.

misconceptions.feedback: A single noun gives a scanner almost nothing, and it fits any page about keys.
This is a slogan, not a name for the content, and the reader cannot tell what it contains.
"Things" says nothing, so the heading cannot guide a scanning reader.

questions.prompt: Five plans each have a price, a user limit and a storage limit. A table has one column for the plan name and one for each attribute. How many columns does it have?
hints: Count the attributes first.
There are three attributes.
Add one column for the plan name.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One column for the name plus three for price, user limit and storage makes 4.

questions.onCorrect: The five plans become five rows, so the table is four columns wide and five rows deep, plus a header row.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the column for the plan's name.
That counts the plans, which are rows, not columns.

questions.prompt: In "The file is saved by the application", which words name the thing that does the saving?
hints: Look after the word "by".
The actor appears at the end of this sentence, where an active sentence would put it first.
questions.onCorrect: In the active version, "The application saves the file", the actor comes first and the sentence is shorter.

misconceptions.feedback: The file is what gets saved. The actor is the thing doing the saving, which this sentence puts after "by".

questions.prompt: A page says "copy the folder", then "open the directory", then "check the location". All three mean one place. How many different things will a careful reader assume the page is talking about?
hints: A careful reader assumes a new word names something new.
Count the different words used.
There are three words: folder, directory and location.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each new word suggests a new thing, so the reader assumes three.

questions.onCorrect: A reader who meets a new word assumes a new thing, so the variation meant for elegance reads as three places.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what the writer meant. The question asks what a careful reader will assume.
Count all three words used: folder, directory and location.

questions.prompt: A pronoun such as "it" or "this" that could point to more than one earlier item is called an ambiguous what?
hints: The word names the part of speech.
questions.onCorrect: The cure is to replace the pronoun with the noun it was meant to stand for.

questions.prompt: Count the passive verbs: "The server is restarted. The cache is cleared and the logs are rotated. Then the service starts."
hints: A passive verb has a form of "to be" and a past participle.
"is restarted" is one. Look for others.
Check "starts": the service does that action itself.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: "is restarted", "is cleared" and "are rotated" are passive. "starts" is active, so the count is 3.

questions.onCorrect: Three of the four verbs hide who restarted, cleared and rotated, which is a lot of unknowns for one short paragraph.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the last sentence: "the service starts" has an actor doing the action, so it is active.
The second sentence has two passive verbs, plus one in the first.

questions.prompt: Which is the active-voice version of "The request is validated by the server"?

choices.label: The server is validating the request.

hints: Put the actor first and make it do the verb.
The actor is the server.
questions.onCorrect: Putting the actor in front of the verb makes the sentence shorter and the responsibility clear.

misconceptions.feedback: This is still passive in effect: the server has disappeared.
This turns the verb into a noun and drops the actor.
The actor is first, but this is a different tense, and it uses a longer verb phrase than the sentence needs.

questions.prompt: "The file is deleted after 30 days" is passive, and it is fine. Passive suits a sentence when the actor is unknown or what?
hints: Does the reader need to know which process deletes the file?
questions.onCorrect: Here the reader needs the rule and not the mechanism, so leaving the actor out gives them what they came for.

questions.prompt: Count the passive verbs: "The form is submitted by the user. The data is checked by the server. If an error is found, a message is shown. The user then edits the form."
hints: Passive verbs combine a form of "to be" with a past participle.
Go through each sentence and note them.
The last sentence has only an active verb.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: "is submitted", "is checked", "is found" and "is shown" are passive, and "edits" is active, so 4.

questions.onCorrect: A count like this is a quick audit: each passive verb is a place where the actor might need to be named.

misconceptions.feedback: The last sentence has one active verb, "edits", so it is not part of the count.
One passive is in the conditional clause: "is found".

questions.prompt: "The script reads the config and writes the log. It fails if missing." Which rewrite fixes the unclear pronoun?

choices.label: The script fails if the config is missing.
It fails if it is missing.
The script reads the config and writes the log, which fails if missing.

hints: Replace the pronoun with the noun you mean.
Decide which thing could be missing: the script, the config or the log?

acceptedIdeas: The script fails if the config is missing.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The script fails if the config is missing.

questions.onCorrect: Naming the noun makes the sentence self-sufficient, so it can be read out of order or in search results.

misconceptions.feedback: Both pronouns are still unclear. They could point to the script, the config or the log.
"This" has no clear noun after it, so the reader still has to guess.
"Which" attaches to the last noun, so it now says the log fails.

questions.prompt: Using one name for one thing throughout a document is called consistent what?
hints: The word means the set of terms used in a field.
questions.onCorrect: Because readers treat a new word as a new thing, a consistent term is as much a fact about the product as the product's behaviour.

questions.prompt: In a good instruction, which comes first: the action or the condition? Compare "To update, open the menu" with "Open the menu to update" and answer with the part that leads.
hints: The reader needs to know whether the instruction applies to them before they act on it.
questions.onCorrect: A reader who has met the condition can skip a step that doesn't apply, instead of doing it and then finding out.

misconceptions.feedback: Leading with the instruction tempts a reader to do it at once. Opening with the "to update" clause lets them check it applies to them.

questions.prompt: Which list is parallel?

choices.label: Install the package; configure the file; run the server
Install the package; configuring the file; run the server

hints: Look at the first word of each item.
All three should begin with the same grammatical form.

acceptedIdeas: Install the package; configure the file; run the server
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Install the package; configure the file; run the server

questions.onCorrect: Parallel items let a reader treat the list as one pattern and see at once what differs.

misconceptions.feedback: The middle item switches to an -ing form, so the three do not read as a set.
Each item takes a different grammatical form.
The items mix nouns and a verb, and two have no action at all.

questions.prompt: Which change raises Flesch reading ease more: cutting the average sentence from 15 to 14 words, or cutting the average word from 1.5 to 1.4 syllables?

choices.label: Cutting the word from 1.5 to 1.4 syllables
Cutting the sentence from 15 to 14 words
They change it by the same amount

hints: Look at the size of each number being multiplied in the formula.
The weight on syllables is far larger than the weight on words.

acceptedIdeas: Cutting the word from 1.5 to 1.4 syllables
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cutting the word from 1.5 to 1.4 syllables

questions.onCorrect: The syllable term has a coefficient of 84.6 against 1.015 for words, so a small change in word length shifts the score a lot.

misconceptions.feedback: One word fewer changes the score by about one point. The other change moves it by more than eight.
The two terms of the formula have very different weights.

questions.prompt: On the Flesch reading ease scale, does a higher score mean the text is easier or harder to read?
hints: The formula subtracts the effect of long sentences and long words.
questions.onCorrect: Higher scores mean easier text, which is why the formula starts from a large number and takes away.

misconceptions.feedback: The formula subtracts for long sentences and long words, so more difficulty lowers the score.

questions.prompt: Finish the calculation: 206.835 − 1.015 × 10 − 84.6 × 1.5. Give the score to the nearest whole number.
hints: First work out 1.015 × 10.
Then work out 84.6 × 1.5.
Subtract both from 206.835.
questions.onCorrect: A text of short sentences can still score modestly if its words are long, which is why both numbers count.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the exact value. The question asks for the nearest whole number.
That subtracts only 126.9 or only the sentence term. Subtract both.

questions.prompt: A passage keeps its 52 words and 1.6 syllables per word, but is cut from one sentence into four of equal length. What is its Flesch score now, to the nearest whole number?
hints: Work out the new words per sentence.
52 ÷ 4 = 13, and the syllables per word stay at 1.6.
Put 13 and 1.6 into the formula.
questions.onCorrect: The same words gave 19 as one sentence, so the split alone lifts the score by about 39 points.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the score of the single long sentence. The question asks for the split version.
That is the word count. The formula needs words per sentence, which is 13.

questions.prompt: "Press Save to keep your work." has 6 words and about 1.17 syllables per word, so use 8 words per sentence and 1.25 syllables per word for a short page of such lines. What is the score, to the nearest whole number?
hints: Multiply 1.015 by 8.
Multiply 84.6 by 1.25.
Subtract both from 206.835.
questions.onCorrect: A score of 93 describes how easy the lines are to read, and says nothing about whether the lines tell the reader the truth.

misconceptions.feedback: That is exact. Give the nearest whole number.
That misses the syllable term, 84.6 × 1.25.

questions.prompt: A text averages 15 words per sentence and 1.5 syllables per word. Using 206.835 − 1.015 × W − 84.6 × S, what is its Flesch reading ease to the nearest whole number?
hints: Work out 1.015 × 15 first.
Then 84.6 × 1.5, and subtract both from 206.835.
Round your result to a whole number.
questions.onCorrect: A score in the 60s is generally taken to be plain English, readable by most adults.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the exact value. Round to the nearest whole number.
That subtracts only the sentence term. Subtract the syllable term as well.

questions.prompt: A text averages 15 words per sentence and 1.4 syllables per word. What is its Flesch reading ease to the nearest whole number?
hints: 84.6 × 1.4 is the syllable term.
1.015 × 15 is the sentence term.
Subtract both from 206.835.
questions.onCorrect: Shortening the words from 1.5 to 1.4 syllables raised the score by more than eight points.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses 1.5 syllables per word. This text has 1.4.
Round to the nearest whole number.

questions.prompt: List items that begin with the same grammatical form, such as three verbs in a row, are said to have what kind of structure?
hints: The items run alongside one another, like lines that never cross.
questions.onCorrect: Parallel items read as a set, so a reader can scan the list and see what differs.

questions.prompt: The first editing pass decides what the reader must do or know, and deletes the rest. What is that pass about: content, structure, or sentences?
hints: The earlier the decision, the more later work it saves.
It comes before order, and before wording.
questions.onCorrect: Cutting content first means no time is spent polishing words that are about to be deleted.

misconceptions.feedback: Those come later. First decide what stays, and only then order it and polish it.

questions.prompt: A 40-word paragraph is edited down to 28 words. How many words were removed?
hints: Subtract the new length from the old.
40 minus 28.
The result is the number of words cut.
questions.onCorrect: Counting words removed is the first measure. The next screen turns it into a percentage, which can be compared across paragraphs.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the length that remains. The question asks for the number removed.

questions.prompt: Words such as "in order to", "it should be noted that" and "very", which add nothing the reader needs, are called what?
hints: They fill space without carrying information.
questions.onCorrect: Filler is easy to spot once you ask of each word what the reader would lose without it.

questions.prompt: A 60-word paragraph is edited down to 45 words. What percentage was removed?
hints: Work out how many words were removed.
Divide that by the original length, 60.
Multiply the result by 100.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 60 − 45 = 15 words removed, and 15 ÷ 60 = 0.25, which is 25%.

questions.onCorrect: Dividing by the original length keeps the percentage honest: the cut is measured against what you started with.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the new length, 45. Divide by the original, 60.
That is the number of words removed. The question asks for a percentage.

questions.prompt: Deleting "Do not" from "Do not delete the backup" makes the sentence shorter and also changes what?
hints: Read the edited sentence and say what it now tells the reader to do.
questions.onCorrect: A cut that removes a warning, a number or a condition changes the facts, so it has to be refused however many words it saves.

questions.prompt: A 50-word paragraph contains 9 words of pure filler and a 5-word warning. You cut the filler and keep the warning. What percentage of the paragraph was removed?
hints: Only the filler is removed.
9 words are removed from a total of 50.
Divide 9 by 50 and multiply by 100.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 9 ÷ 50 = 0.18, which is 18%. The warning stays.

questions.onCorrect: A careful edit often cuts less than it could, because every word that carries a fact stays.

misconceptions.feedback: That removes the warning too: (9 + 5) ÷ 50. The warning has to stay.
That is the number of words, not a percentage.

questions.prompt: A paragraph is cut from 40 words to 28. What percentage was removed?
hints: Find the number of words removed.
Divide by the original length, 40.
Convert the decimal to a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 40 − 28 = 12 words removed, and 12 ÷ 40 = 0.3, which is 30%.

questions.onCorrect: Percentages let you compare edits of paragraphs of different lengths.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the percentage that remains. The question asks for the percentage removed.
That is the number of words, not a percentage.

questions.prompt: An 80-word section is edited down to 62 words. What percentage was removed? Give the answer to one decimal place.
hints: Subtract to find the words removed.
Divide by the original 80.
Multiply by 100.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 80 − 62 = 18 words removed, and 18 ÷ 80 = 0.225, which is 22.5%.

questions.onCorrect: A cut near a fifth to a quarter is common for a first draft with real padding in it.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the new length, 62. Divide by the original length.
That is the word count removed. The question asks for the percentage.

questions.prompt: Which cut changes the meaning, and should be refused?

choices.label: Deleting "Do not" from "Do not unplug the drive"
Changing "at this point in time" to "now"

hints: Ask whether the reader could now do something wrong.
A negative, a number or a condition is a fact.

acceptedIdeas: Deleting "Do not" from "Do not unplug the drive"
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Deleting "Do not" from "Do not unplug the drive"

questions.onCorrect: Edits must preserve facts. Words that carry a warning, number or condition stay, however short the page gets.

misconceptions.feedback: This keeps every fact. It only removes words that carry nothing.
"Very" adds emphasis but no fact the reader can act on.
The two mean the same, and the shorter one is clearer.

questions.prompt: In the step "In the File menu, click Save", what does the reader learn first: the location or the action?
hints: Read the step up to the first comma.
questions.onCorrect: The reader's eyes are on the screen, so telling them where to look before what to do saves a search.

misconceptions.feedback: The action comes second here. The step opens with the place, so the reader looks there first.

questions.prompt: A step reads: "Open the Admin panel, choose Users, select the account and click Reset." How many steps should it be split into?
hints: Count the verbs the reader must carry out.
Open, choose, select and click.
Each action gets its own number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are four actions: open, choose, select and click, so four steps.

questions.onCorrect: One action per step lets the reader do it, check it and place themselves in the list.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how the step was written. The question asks how many it should be.
Count all four verbs: open, choose, select and click.

questions.prompt: What the reader needs before step 1, such as access, tools and software versions, is listed as the procedure's what?
hints: It is the word for what must be true before you begin.
questions.onCorrect: Putting them first means a reader finds out they lack a tool before they have half-changed their system.

questions.prompt: After the step "Click Deploy", which addition helps the reader most?

choices.label: The status changes to Running within 30 seconds.

hints: The reader wants to know whether it worked.
Pick the addition that names something they can see.

acceptedIdeas: The status changes to Running within 30 seconds.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The status changes to Running within 30 seconds.

questions.onCorrect: A stated result with a time lets the reader tell success from failure, and says when to start worrying.

misconceptions.feedback: This is true of most steps, but it gives the reader nothing to check on screen.
A vague caution doesn't say what to look for or what could go wrong.
This leaves the reader waiting without knowing how long or for what.

questions.prompt: A step reads: "Log in, open Billing, choose Invoices, download the latest one and email it to finance." How many numbered steps does it become?
hints: List each verb the reader must perform.
Log in, open, choose, download, email.
One step for each.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Log in, open, choose, download and email are five actions, so five steps.

questions.onCorrect: Five short steps are longer to read than one sentence, but each can be done and checked on its own.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the original count. Split it by action.
Count "log in" as an action too.

questions.prompt: "If the status is red, restart the service." Which part of this step comes first for the reader: the condition or the action?
hints: Read the words before the comma.
questions.onCorrect: A reader who is told the condition first can skip a step that doesn't apply to them, instead of restarting a healthy service.

misconceptions.feedback: The action is second here. The sentence opens with "If the status is red", which tells the reader when the step applies.

questions.prompt: "Open Settings, select Network, and click Reset." How many steps should this be?
hints: Count the actions the reader has to carry out.
The verbs are open, select and click.
Each gets one numbered step.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Open, select and click are three actions, so three steps.

questions.onCorrect: With three steps, a failure at step 3 shows that steps 1 and 2 worked.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how it is written. The question asks how many steps it should become.

questions.prompt: Which wording follows "location first"?

choices.label: Click Save in the File menu.
In the File menu, click Save.
Save is in the File menu, click it.

hints: The reader's eyes need to be in the right place before they act.
Pick the one that starts with where.

acceptedIdeas: In the File menu, click Save.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In the File menu, click Save.

questions.onCorrect: Telling the reader where to look first saves them hunting for a Save button across a whole screen.

misconceptions.feedback: This puts the action first, so the reader must read to the end to learn where to look.
This is a statement followed by a second action, and it uses a pronoun.
This is a fragment with no verb telling the reader what to do.

questions.prompt: What the reader should see after a step, so they know it worked, is called the expected what?
hints: It is what the screen shows when things go right.
questions.onCorrect: Without an expected result the reader can't tell success from silent failure.

questions.prompt: A 40-line sample makes one point, and the point needs only 8 of its lines. How many lines should be removed?
hints: Subtract the lines the point needs from the total.
40 lines in all, 8 needed.
Take 8 from 40.
questions.onCorrect: Those 32 lines may be useful in a real program, but each one is something the reader must read and rule out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of lines to keep. The question asks how many to remove.

questions.prompt: A Python sample calls json.loads without importing json. Python reports an error whose name begins with "Name". What is it?
hints: Python says it doesn't know the name json.
The error class is named after what is wrong.
questions.onCorrect: NameError means a name was used before it was defined or imported, which is exactly what a missing import produces.

misconceptions.feedback: An ImportError comes from a failed import statement. Here there is no import at all, so Python never tries.

questions.prompt: A sample that works when copied, with its imports and setup included, is called what kind of sample?
hints: It can be run exactly as it appears.
questions.onCorrect: A runnable sample is tested at each release, since software changes and an untested sample slowly stops working.

questions.prompt: After this code runs, what number is printed? import json / data = json.loads('{"a": 1, "b": 2}') / print(data['b'])
hints: The import makes json available.
json.loads turns the string into a dictionary with keys a and b.
data['b'] is the value stored under b.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: data['b'] looks up the key b in {"a": 1, "b": 2}, which is 2.

questions.onCorrect: Showing this output beside the code lets the reader check their own run against it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value under the key a. The code prints the value under b.

questions.prompt: A sample teaches how to set a timeout. Which line is least relevant?

choices.label: import logging  (for a feature the sample never uses)

hints: Ask what the reader would lose if the line was removed.
Three of these lines serve the timeout.

acceptedIdeas: import logging  (for a feature the sample never uses)
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: import logging  (for a feature the sample never uses)

questions.onCorrect: A line that the point doesn't need is a line the reader has to read, wonder about and rule out.

misconceptions.feedback: This line is the point of the sample.
This line uses the client, so the timeout has something to apply to.
This shows the reader a result, so they can check their run.

questions.prompt: The sample data = json.loads('{"a": 1}') followed by print(data['a']) fails when run alone. Which line must be added first? Type it.
hints: The first line uses the name json, but nothing has defined it yet.
In Python, a module is made available with an import statement.
questions.onCorrect: A sample that omits its import works only in the writer's session, which is why runnable samples are tested.

misconceptions.feedback: The module is named json, but the line needed is the statement that imports it.

questions.prompt: A sample is trimmed from 40 lines to 10. What percentage of its lines was removed?
hints: Subtract the new length from the old.
Divide the lines removed by 40.
Multiply by 100.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 40 − 10 = 30 lines removed, and 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75, which is 75%.

questions.onCorrect: Trimming this far is common, since a sample serves one point and real code carries many.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the percentage that remains. The question asks for the percentage removed.
That is the number of lines, not a percentage.

questions.prompt: Which Authorization header is best for a documentation sample?
hints: A stand-in should say what value the reader must supply.
Which option is both obviously fake and self-explanatory?
questions.onCorrect: A name such as YOUR_API_KEY is obviously not a real secret and tells the reader exactly what to replace.

misconceptions.feedback: This looks like a real secret, and readers may paste it as it is or learn the format wrongly.
"foo" doesn't tell the reader what to put there.
The dots say nothing about what is missing, and the line won't run as written.

questions.prompt: A value such as YOUR_API_KEY that the reader has to replace with their own is called a what?
hints: It stands in for a real value.
questions.onCorrect: A stand-in is labelled with what it stands for, so the reader never has to guess what goes there.

questions.prompt: A reader asks what happens if they leave the retries option out. Which column of the parameter table answers that? Name the column.
hints: The value that applies when the reader does not set the parameter.
questions.onCorrect: The default is often the very thing a reader looks up, so it gets a column of its own.

misconceptions.feedback: "Required" says whether the reader must set it. The column asked about holds the value used when they set nothing.

questions.prompt: A reference entry for a function shows its name, purpose, returns and example. The template has six fields: name, purpose, parameters, returns, errors and example. How many fields does this entry lack?
hints: Count the fields the entry has.
It has four of the six.
Subtract from six.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6 − 4 = 2 fields are missing: parameters and errors.

questions.onCorrect: A missing field is a place where a reader looks and finds nothing, and they can't tell whether the answer is "none" or "unwritten".

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of fields present. The question asks for the number missing.

questions.prompt: The timeout row gives the value 30. What must the description say so the reader knows what the 30 counts: the minutes, the seconds, or in general the what?
hints: 30 of what?
questions.onCorrect: A number without a unit forces the reader to guess whether 30 means seconds or milliseconds, and a wrong guess can look like a bug.

questions.prompt: A request fails every time. The retries parameter has its default of 3, meaning the failed request is tried again 3 times before an error is raised. How many times in total is the request sent?
hints: Retries come after the first attempt.
Count the first attempt, then each retry.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first attempt plus 3 retries is 4 requests in total.

questions.onCorrect: This is why a description should say exactly what is counted: "retries" and "attempts" differ by one.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the retries. The original request makes one more.
The first attempt is one request and the retries are three more, not four.

questions.prompt: Which description is best for the timeout parameter?

choices.label: The number of seconds to wait for a response before the request fails.

hints: A good description gives the unit and the effect.
Pick the one that says what is counted and what happens at the end.

acceptedIdeas: The number of seconds to wait for a response before the request fails.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The number of seconds to wait for a response before the request fails.

questions.onCorrect: A description that names the unit and the consequence lets the reader use the parameter without reading anything else.

misconceptions.feedback: This doesn't say how long what, or in which unit.
This repeats the name and adds nothing.
This doesn't state a unit or what the time is for.

questions.prompt: A reference page has 12 entries. 9 of them have all six fields, and the others each lack one. How many entries need fixing?
hints: Subtract the complete entries from the total.
12 entries in all, 9 complete.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 − 9 = 3 entries need a missing field added.

questions.onCorrect: Checking every entry against the template is a quick review, and a script can do it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number already complete. The question asks how many need fixing.

questions.prompt: A parameter row lists name, type, default and description. Which column does it lack, the one that tells the reader whether they must supply the value?
hints: The answer is yes or no for each parameter.
questions.onCorrect: Without it a reader can't tell which parameters they can safely leave out.

misconceptions.feedback: The default is already in the row. The missing column says whether the parameter is compulsory.

questions.prompt: A parameter row lists name, type and description only. Which fields would a reader most need added?
hints: Think of what a reader asks about an option: do I have to set it, and what if I don't?
Pick the pair that answers both.
questions.onCorrect: Whether a parameter is required and what it defaults to are the two facts a reader most often looks up.

misconceptions.feedback: These help maintainers but not a reader looking up how to use the parameter.
Presentation isn't information about the parameter.
The licence belongs to the whole project, not to each parameter.

questions.prompt: An entry has a name, a purpose and a parameters table, and nothing else. The template has six fields. How many fields does it lack?
hints: Count the fields it has.
It has three of the six.
Subtract from six.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6 − 3 = 3 fields are missing: returns, errors and example.

questions.onCorrect: A reader who finds no errors field can't tell whether the function never fails or the writer didn't say.

misconceptions.feedback: The entry has three fields, so three are missing.

questions.prompt: In "GET /v1/items/{id}", the word GET names the HTTP what, which says what kind of operation is requested?
hints: GET, POST, PUT and DELETE are all examples.
questions.onCorrect: The method and path together identify an endpoint, so the page title should carry both.

questions.prompt: A DELETE request succeeds and the server has nothing to send back. Which status code, as a number, usually signals that?
hints: It is in the 2xx family, because the request worked.
Nothing is returned, so the code says so.
Its name is No Content.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 204 No Content means success with no response body.

questions.onCorrect: A 204 response has no body at all, so the page should show a status line and nothing beneath it.

misconceptions.feedback: 200 OK normally comes with a body. When there is nothing to return, a more exact success code exists.
404 means the thing wasn't found, which is a failure.

questions.prompt: A POST to /v1/items is sent without the required name. The server rejects it as a malformed request from the client. Which status code?
hints: The mistake is the client's, so the code is in the 4xx family.
The request itself is invalid.
Its name is Bad Request.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 400 Bad Request means the client sent something the server can't process.

questions.onCorrect: A 400 should carry a body saying which field was wrong, so the reader can fix it without guessing.

misconceptions.feedback: 422 is used by some APIs for a well-formed request with invalid content. For a missing field, the more general code is the common choice.
A 500 means the server failed. Here the client sent a bad request.

questions.prompt: The reader's API key has expired. The request lacks valid credentials. Which status code?
hints: The request can't prove who it is.
The code is in the 4xx family and starts with 40.
Its name is Unauthorized.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 401 means the request lacks valid credentials, and an expired key is no longer valid.

questions.onCorrect: A 401 tells the client to authenticate again. A 403 means the credentials are fine but the action is not allowed.

misconceptions.feedback: 403 means the credentials are valid but not permitted. An expired key is not valid at all.

questions.prompt: GET /v1/items/{id} is called with an id that does not exist. Which status code?
hints: The request was well formed, but the thing isn't there.
Not found.
Its name says exactly that.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 404 Not Found means the server has no resource at that path.

questions.onCorrect: A 404 should say which item was looked for, because the id in the path may itself be a typo.

misconceptions.feedback: The request was well formed. It simply names something that isn't there.
204 is a success. Nothing exists at this path.

questions.prompt: The OpenAPI snippet in the figure lists the responses for POST /v1/items. How many response codes does it declare?
hints: Look under the responses line.
Each quoted number is one declared response.
There are four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It declares 201, 400, 401 and 403, which is four.

questions.onCorrect: A generated reference built from this file lists all four, but the prose around it still has to say what the reader does about each.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only the success response. The snippet declares more.
Count the quoted codes again: 201, 400, 401 and 403.

questions.prompt: A 429 response often includes a header that tells the client how many seconds to wait before trying again. What is that header called?
hints: Its name says what the client should do and when.
questions.onCorrect: Documenting this header once, in a rate-limits section, saves repeating it on every endpoint.

questions.prompt: What status code means the client has sent too many requests?
hints: It is in the 4xx family, because the client is sending too often.
It is a code for rate limiting.
Its name is Too Many Requests.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 429 Too Many Requests is the rate-limit response.

questions.onCorrect: 429 comes from RFC 6585 and is often accompanied by a Retry-After header.

misconceptions.feedback: 503 means the server is unavailable. A rate limit is aimed at one client sending too much.
403 means not permitted, which is different from too many requests.

questions.prompt: What status code does a successful POST that creates a resource usually return?
hints: It is a 2xx code, because the request succeeded.
It names a more exact success than 200.
Its name is Created.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 201 Created confirms the resource now exists.

questions.onCorrect: The response also usually includes the new item, or a Location header pointing to it.

misconceptions.feedback: 200 OK is a general success. For a request that creates something, a code named Created is more exact.
204 means success with nothing to return, but a created item is normally returned.

questions.prompt: A valid key without permission to delete an item calls DELETE. Which status fits?
hints: The credentials are fine, so what is wrong?
Valid but not permitted.
questions.onCorrect: 403 Forbidden says the server knows who you are and still refuses, so the fix is permission, not a new key.

misconceptions.feedback: 401 means the credentials are missing or invalid. Here the key is valid.
404 means the resource wasn't found. The item exists.
429 means too many requests, which is a different problem.

questions.prompt: A proposed change that teammates review and approve before it is merged into the main branch is called a pull request. What is the usual short form, or the full name, of it?
hints: The author asks the project to pull in their change.
questions.onCorrect: Putting a docs change and its code change in one pull request lets the reviewer see that they agree.

questions.prompt: A linter reports 14 issues across 2,000 words of documentation. How many issues is that per 1,000 words?
hints: Work out how many thousands of words there are.
2,000 words is two lots of 1,000.
Divide 14 by 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 14 ÷ 2 = 7 issues per 1,000 words.

questions.onCorrect: A rate per 1,000 words lets you compare a large manual with a short page.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total. Divide it by the number of thousands of words.
That multiplies instead of dividing. There are two lots of 1,000 words, so divide.

questions.prompt: A how-to has 12 commands. A proofreader finds no errors. Someone then runs all 12 commands, and 11 succeed. How many failed?
hints: Subtract the successes from the total.
12 commands, 11 succeeded.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 − 11 = 1 command failed, and proofreading did not find it.

questions.onCorrect: A missing flag reads perfectly well, so only running the steps shows it.

misconceptions.feedback: The proofreader found none, but running the steps found one failure.
That is the number that succeeded. The question asks how many failed.

questions.prompt: A release fixes a bug in how dates are parsed. Under which Keep a Changelog heading does the entry go?
hints: Think about what the change means for a user, and pick the heading that says so.
questions.onCorrect: "Fixed" is for bugs that users could hit. A heading that says what changed for them saves them reading every entry.

misconceptions.feedback: "Changed" is for changes in existing behaviour that users will notice. A bug fix has its own heading.

questions.prompt: A changelog is written for whom: the developers who wrote the code, or the people who use it? Name the group.
hints: Who wants to know what changed for them?
questions.onCorrect: A changelog says what changed for the user and not what the developers typed, which is why it is not a copy of the commit log.

misconceptions.feedback: The commit log is written for developers. The changelog is for the people who use the product.

questions.prompt: A release has 7 changelog entries: 3 under Added, 2 under Fixed, 1 under Removed and the rest under Changed. How many are under Changed?
hints: Find how many entries are already sorted.
Add up the entries that are already sorted.
Subtract that sum from 7.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 7 − (3 + 2 + 1) = 1 entry under Changed.

questions.onCorrect: Counting entries per heading shows at a glance whether a release is mostly new features or mostly fixes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number already sorted into the other headings.
Seven entries, and six are accounted for, so one is left.

questions.prompt: Which line belongs in a changelog for users?
hints: Choose the line a user could act on.
It names what changed and what to do.
questions.onCorrect: A good entry says what changed and, if the user must do something, what to do instead.

misconceptions.feedback: This is a commit message about code, with no change a user can see.
A commit message like this describes the developer's process, not the user's experience.
This records source control activity, not what changed for a user.

questions.prompt: A release removes an endpoint. Under which Keep a Changelog heading does the entry go?
hints: Think about what the change means for a user, and pick the heading that says so.
questions.onCorrect: A removal is the change that most often breaks a user, so it is easiest to find under its own heading.

misconceptions.feedback: Deprecated is a warning that something will go in a future release. This endpoint is already gone.

questions.prompt: Which review check catches a missing flag in a command?
hints: Which check would fail if the command were wrong?
The check has to exercise the commands.
questions.onCorrect: A review that runs every command finds what proofreading misses, because the page reads fine and the command fails.

misconceptions.feedback: A spell-checker reads words. A missing flag is spelled correctly.
Headings show structure but not whether a command works.
A word count measures length, not correctness.

questions.prompt: A tool that automatically checks text against a style guide's rules is called a what?
hints: The word comes from checking code for small faults.
questions.onCorrect: A linter turns style-guide rules into checks that run on every change, so a human reviewer can spend time on whether the steps work.

questions.prompt: Instead of asking a reader whether a page is clear, what do you do during a test: ask them, or what? Complete: you ___ whether they finish the task.
hints: The test is about behaviour, not opinion.
questions.onCorrect: Watching shows where the page fails, while a reader's opinion of clarity is rarely accurate about what they didn't understand.

misconceptions.feedback: Asking brings polite answers. What reveals the fault is watching what the reader does.

questions.prompt: 6 of 8 testers finish the task. What is the task success rate as a percentage?
hints: Divide the number who finished by the number who tried.
6 divided by 8.
Multiply the decimal by 100.
questions.onCorrect: The rate divides finishers by everyone who attempted it, including those who gave up.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number who finished, not a percentage.
That is the percentage who did not finish. The question asks for success.

questions.prompt: In the figure, 10 testers start and 2 stop at step 4. How many testers reach step 5?
hints: Two of the ten stopped at step 4.
Subtract them from the ten.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10 − 2 = 8 testers are still going at step 5.

questions.onCorrect: The step where the count drops is the first point of failure, and it is where to look first.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number who stopped. The question asks for those who remain.
Two of them stopped at step 4, so fewer than ten remain.

questions.prompt: Participants who finish the task divided by participants who attempted it is called the task success what?
hints: It is expressed as a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: A rate is only meaningful with the count behind it: 80% of 10 testers is 8 people.

questions.prompt: 9 of 15 testers finish the task. What is the success rate as a percentage?
hints: Divide the finishers by the attempts.
9 divided by 15.
Multiply by 100.
questions.onCorrect: At 60%, four in ten readers fail, and the step where they stop is where to start.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the failure rate, 6 of 15. The question asks for success.
That is the count. Convert it to a percentage.

questions.prompt: Support receives 30 tickets a month about one error. After the error is added to the troubleshooting page, tickets fall to 6 a month. By what percentage did they fall?
hints: Find how many fewer tickets there are.
24 fewer out of the original 30.
Divide by 30 and multiply by 100.
questions.onCorrect: Support tickets are a signal that keeps coming after release, and they let you measure whether a fix worked.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the percentage that remains. The question asks for the fall.
That is the number of tickets, not a percentage.

questions.prompt: A page gets few views, but readers keep asking questions it answers. The page may be needed and still hard to locate. What word describes a page that readers can locate when they need it?
hints: The cause may be the title, the navigation or search terms.
questions.onCorrect: Low page views alone don't show that a page is unneeded. Search terms and tickets show whether readers look for what it says.

misconceptions.feedback: Few views might mean the page is not needed, but it might mean readers can't find it. Check what they search for.

questions.prompt: 8 of 10 testers finish a task. What is the task success rate as a percentage?
hints: Divide the number who finished by the number who attempted.
8 divided by 10.
Multiply by 100.
questions.onCorrect: The other two testers stopped at step 4 because the page assumed a tool was installed, so the 80% points at a fix.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count. Convert it to a percentage.
That is the percentage who failed. The question asks for success.

questions.prompt: 6 testers stop at step 4 and 1 stops at step 7. Which fix first?
hints: Count the readers stopped at each point.
Fix where the most readers stopped.
questions.onCorrect: Fixing the failure that stops the most readers raises the success rate the fastest.

misconceptions.feedback: Fewer readers stopped there, so a fix helps fewer people.
Nobody stopped at the title, so it isn't the failure the test found.
Fonts didn't stop anyone, and the test shows the real faults.

questions.prompt: Of 10 testers, 6 stop at step 4 and 1 stops at step 7. How many finish the task?
hints: Subtract those who stopped at step 4.
Then subtract the one who stopped at step 7.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10 − 6 − 1 = 3 testers finish.

questions.onCorrect: The success rate is therefore 30%, and most of the lost readers can be won back by one fix.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the reader who stopped at step 7.
That is the number who stopped at step 7. Subtract both groups from 10.

flashcards.front: Name the three parts of a one-sentence audience statement.
flashcards.back: Who the reader is, what they are trying to do, and what they already know.

flashcards.front: A statement already names the reader and the goal. Which part is still missing if it says nothing about prior experience?
flashcards.back: The starting knowledge, because it decides which steps the page must spell out.

flashcards.front: Why does writing for "everyone" fail?
flashcards.back: A page needs one primary reader to decide what to include, and other readers can be pointed elsewhere by links.

flashcards.front: What does a tutorial leave out on purpose?
flashcards.back: Options and edge cases, because a beginner needs one clear path to build confidence.

flashcards.front: Which framework names the four kinds of page: tutorial, how-to guide, reference and explanation?
flashcards.back: Diátaxis, by Daniele Procida, sorts documentation by what the reader needs.

flashcards.front: Which kind of page gives steps to a reader who already has the basic skill?
flashcards.back: A how-to guide serves one goal for someone who can already do the basics.

flashcards.front: Why does the heading "Things to know" fail a scanning reader?
flashcards.back: It names nothing, so a reader scanning the headings cannot tell whether the answer is under it.

flashcards.front: What is it called when you put the main point or action first in a page, section or sentence?
flashcards.back: Front-loading puts what the scanning reader needs where they will look first.

flashcards.front: Which list type suits steps that must be done in order?
flashcards.back: Numbers give each step a place the reader can return to.

flashcards.front: Which voice puts the actor first, as in "The server validates the request"?
flashcards.back: Active voice names who acts, so the reader knows who does what.

flashcards.front: Why is varying "folder", "directory" and "location" a mistake in documentation?
flashcards.back: A new word suggests a new thing, so a reader may think there are three places.

flashcards.front: Which plain verb replaces "utilize"?
flashcards.back: "Use" is shorter, and a reader meets it every day.

flashcards.front: Is text with a higher Flesch reading ease score easier or harder to read? Answer with one word.
flashcards.back: Easier text, because the formula subtracts for long sentences and long words.

flashcards.front: In which year did Rudolf Flesch publish the Reading Ease formula that the course uses?
flashcards.back: He published it in 1948, and its coefficients are 206.835, 1.015 and 84.6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: He published it in 1948, and its coefficients are 206.835, 1.015 and 84.6.

flashcards.front: Why should a condition come before an action in an instruction?
flashcards.back: The reader can check whether the instruction applies to them before they do anything.

flashcards.front: Name the four editing passes in order.
flashcards.back: Content, structure, sentences and words, then names, numbers and links; separating them stops fixes in one from hiding faults in another.

flashcards.front: Words that add nothing the reader needs, such as "it should be noted that", are called what?
flashcards.back: Filler. Cutting it leaves every fact in place and shortens the page.

flashcards.front: A 20-word sentence is edited to 15 words. What percentage was removed?
flashcards.back: 5 of 20 words were removed, and 5 ÷ 20 is 25%.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 of 20 words were removed, and 5 ÷ 20 is 25%.

flashcards.front: Why should each numbered step ask for one action?
flashcards.back: If a step fails, the reader can tell which action failed and where to restart.

flashcards.front: What goes before step 1 in a procedure: access, tools and software versions?
flashcards.back: The prerequisites tell the reader what they need before they begin.

flashcards.front: In a step that has a location and an action, which comes first?
flashcards.back: The location, as in "In the File menu, click Save".

flashcards.front: What is the name for a value such as YOUR_API_KEY that the reader must replace?
flashcards.back: A stand-in tells the reader what to supply and can't be mistaken for a real secret.

flashcards.front: Why must a published code sample be tested each release?
flashcards.back: Software changes, so an untested sample slowly stops working, and the reader blames themselves.

flashcards.front: A sample uses json.loads with no import line. What error does Python report?
flashcards.back: It reports NameError, because the name json has not been defined.

flashcards.front: Which parameter-row column tells the reader what happens when they leave a parameter out?
flashcards.back: The default, because it is often the fact the reader came to find.

flashcards.front: Why must a reference entry give a unit for a number such as 30?
flashcards.back: Without a unit the reader has to guess whether 30 means seconds or milliseconds.

flashcards.front: Name the six fields of the reference entry template, in order.
flashcards.back: Name, purpose, parameters, returns, errors and example, in the same order for every entry.

flashcards.front: What does a 401 status mean, and how does a 403 differ?
flashcards.back: 401 means the request lacks valid credentials; 403 means the credentials are valid but not permitted.

flashcards.front: Which status code means Not Found?
flashcards.back: 404 is the response when nothing exists at the requested path.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 404 is the response when nothing exists at the requested path.

flashcards.front: What status code usually follows a POST that creates a resource?
flashcards.back: 201 Created confirms that the resource now exists.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 201 Created confirms that the resource now exists.

flashcards.front: Name the six headings of a Keep a Changelog release.
flashcards.back: Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed and Security; they sort changes by what they mean for users.

flashcards.front: What do you call a tool that checks text automatically against a style guide?
flashcards.back: A linter runs on every change and reports rule breaks, so reviewers needn't catch them by hand.

flashcards.front: Why is proofreading not enough to review a how-to?
flashcards.back: A command can read well and still fail, so a review has to run the steps.

flashcards.front: Why does a test with a real reader find faults that proofreading misses?
flashcards.back: The reader follows the page without the author's knowledge, so skipped steps and unclear terms stop them.

flashcards.front: What do you call the share of participants who finish a task out of those who attempted it?
flashcards.back: It is the task success rate, finishers divided by attempts.
